mcus.name: Apollo3 Blue
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 48 MHz (96 MHz burst) Cortex-M4F with BLE 5.0, 1 MB flash and 384 KB SRAM at about 6 uA/MHz, suited to coin-cell wearables, voice and TinyML. Use the SparkFun Artemis module to avoid the BGA.
notes: The bare chip is a 5x5 mm, 0.5 mm-pitch 81-ball BGA (a 66-ball WLCSP also exists), so hand assembly is impractical. WRL-15484 is SparkFun's Artemis module (15.5 x 10.5 x 2.3 mm, 59 pads in two staggered 1.0 mm-pitch rows, FCC/IC/CE certified, 48 GPIO). Ambiq's 2023 brief also lists a QFN-64 (AMA3B1KK-KQR-B0), but stock is scarce.
48 MHz is the nominal clock and 96 MHz is TurboSPOT burst mode. BLE 5.0 runs on a separate, dedicated controller core that is not user-programmable.

The six IOM masters are each I2C or SPI (6 total, shared), and there is an extra I2C/SPI slave (IOS). MSPI is a separate 1/2/4/8-bit SPI for external flash/PSRAM: XIP up to 64 MB and a memory-mapped PSRAM window of 16 MB.
The I2S port is slave-only and meant for PDM-microphone pass-through, not a general codec interface, so i2s is 0. Stereo PDM mic input is supported.
The ADC is 14-bit with 15 selectable inputs: 10 external single-ended pins (2 differential pairs) plus the temperature sensor and supply channels.
8 CTIMERs give 16 independent PWM outputs. SparkFun lists 31 PWM-capable pins on Artemis.

The 6 uA/MHz is Ambiq's headline figure; CoreMark from flash at 48 MHz measures 10.3 uA/MHz. deepSleepUa is deep sleep at 3.3 V with 8 KB SRAM retained, XTAL/RTC on and BLE off (4.1 uA with all 384 KB retained).

The factory Secure Bootloader (SBL) supports UART wired updates at 115200 baud, selected by a boot pin configured in INFO0 (pin 47 on Artemis). SparkFun's SVL is a faster flash-resident bootloader installed on top. Secure boot plus an AES-128 engine count as crypto.
Arduino support is the SparkFun Arduino_Apollo3 core (v2, Mbed OS based; last release 2022, so effectively maintenance-only). Zephyr support is upstream (apollo3_evb).

mcus.name: AT32F403A
mcus.description: 240 MHz Cortex-M4F with up to 1 MB flash and 224 KB SRAM, crystal-less USB FS, 2x CAN, 2x SDIO and 8 UARTs; a fast, cheap STM32F103/F303 upgrade.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: AT32 Firmware Library (AT32 IDE / Keil / IAR)

notes: Only 256 KB of flash is zero-wait; the rest runs with wait states. SRAM is 96 KB by default, up to 224 KB if zero-wait flash is reduced to 128 KB (user system data).
USB is full-speed device only (crystal-less), no host. SPIM maps up to 16 MB of external quad-SPI flash for code/data.
48-pin parts: 7 UARTs, one 4-bit SDIO, no XMC; XMC/8080 LCD interface needs LQFP-64 (8-bit) or LQFP-100.
Pin-compatible with STM32F103/GD32F303 footprints but not register-compatible; use Artery's firmware library. Standard Arm SWD/JTAG probes work (AT-Link is Artery's own).
ROM bootloader: USB DFU and USART1/USART2 via BOOT0. Deepsleep current is high (~1.3 mA); standby is ~6.5 uA.

mcus.name: AT32F415
mcus.description: Cheap 150 MHz Cortex-M4 with USB FS OTG (host/device) and DFU bootloader, CAN, SDIO and 5 UARTs from about $1.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: AT32 Firmware Library (AT32 IDE / Keil / IAR)

notes: Cortex-M4 without FPU (DSP instructions only).
USB OTG FS with on-chip PHY and a crystal-less mode; ROM bootloader supports USB DFU and USART1/USART2.
48/32-pin parts have 3 USARTs and 10 ADC channels; 5 UARTs and 16 ADC channels need LQFP-64. A 7x7 mm LQFP-64 (-7 suffix) also exists.
Not register-compatible with STM32; use Artery's firmware library. Standard Arm SWD/JTAG probes work.

mcus.name: AT32F421
mcus.description: Value 120 MHz Cortex-M4 with up to 64 KB flash, 2 USART/I2C/SPI and a comparator for under $0.90; a fast STM32F030/G030 alternative.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: AT32 Firmware Library (AT32 IDE / Keil / IAR)

notes: Cortex-M4 without FPU. No USB, no CAN. I2S is half-duplex and shares pins with SPI.
TSSOP-20 parts have 1 USART + 1 UART and 1 SPI; x8 = 64 KB flash / 16 KB SRAM, x4 = 16 KB / 8 KB.
ROM bootloader on USART1/USART2 via BOOT0; standard Arm SWD probes work. Use Artery's firmware library (not register-compatible with STM32).

mcus.name: ESP32
mcus.description: The classic dual-core 240 MHz Wi-Fi + Bluetooth Classic/BLE SoC; huge community, Ethernet MAC, CAN, SD host and cheap pre-certified WROOM modules.
notes: No native USB: needs a USB-UART bridge (CP2102/CH340) plus the DTR/RTS auto-reset circuit for flashing.
Strapping pins GPIO0, 2, 5, 12 (MTDI selects flash voltage) and 15; GPIO34-39 are input-only; GPIO6-11 are wired to the SPI flash.
ADC2 channels cannot be used while Wi-Fi is active.
Bare chip needs external QSPI flash, a 40 MHz crystal and RF matching; most designs use the WROOM-32E module (3.0-3.6 V with its 3.3 V flash).
Only 4 MB of PSRAM is mapped at once; 8 MB needs the himem API. WROVER modules use GPIO16/17 for PSRAM.
Use chip revision v3 (D0WD-V3 / WROOM-32E); older revisions have errata and are not supported by esp-hal (Rust).
PWM count = 16 LED-PWM channels + 2 MCPWM units x 6 outputs.

mcus.name: ESP32-S2
mcus.description: Single-core 240 MHz Wi-Fi SoC with native USB OTG, lots of GPIO and touch pins; good for USB gadgets that need Wi-Fi but not Bluetooth.
notes: No Bluetooth at all, and no FPU (floating point is software-emulated).
Native USB 1.1 OTG (TinyUSB device/host); the ROM can flash over USB (DFU/CDC) as well as UART.
ESP32-S2FN4R2 has a larger exposed pad (4.6 mm) than the other QFN56 variants (4.0 mm).
Strapping pins GPIO0, GPIO45 and GPIO46; bare chips need a 40 MHz crystal and RF matching.
Datasheet quotes up to 1 GB external memory address space, but ESP-IDF supports at most 16 MB flash; up to 10.5 MB PSRAM can be mapped.
ESP32-S2-MINI-2 uses the same 65-pad land pattern as the MINI-1 (KiCad ESP32-S2-MINI-1 footprint).

mcus.name: ESP32-S3
mcus.description: Dual-core 240 MHz Wi-Fi + BLE 5 SoC with native USB, camera/LCD interfaces, vector instructions for AI and up to 16 MB octal PSRAM; the go-to ESP32 for new designs.
notes: USB OTG (FS) and the USB Serial/JTAG controller share one internal PHY, so only one is on the USB pins at a time.
Octal PSRAM/flash (S3R8, -R8/-R16 modules) takes GPIO33-37; on WROOM-1 N16R8 IO35-37 are unavailable (33 usable GPIO).
Strapping pins GPIO0, GPIO3, GPIO45 and GPIO46; bare chips need a 40 MHz crystal and RF matching.
S3R8 octal-PSRAM parts are rated only to 65 °C ambient (85 °C with PSRAM ECC enabled).
Datasheet quotes up to 1 GB external memory space; 32 MB octal-flash modules exist, PSRAM up to 16 MB in-package.
PWM count = 8 LED-PWM channels + 2 MCPWM units x 6 outputs.

mcus.name: ESP32-C2 (ESP8684)
mcus.description: Cheapest Espressif Wi-Fi + BLE 5 chip: 120 MHz RISC-V with in-package flash in a tiny 4x4 mm QFN; an ESP8266 replacement for simple connected devices.
notes: Only sold with 2 or 4 MB flash in the package; there is no external flash or PSRAM interface.
Wi-Fi is 20 MHz-only 802.11n (max 72 Mbps). Needs a 26 or 40 MHz crystal.
No native USB: flash over UART0 with a USB-UART bridge; strapping pins GPIO8 and GPIO9.
Arduino-ESP32 supports the C2 only as an ESP-IDF component / custom lib build, not from the board manager.
The 'X' parts (chip revision v2.0) replace the original ESP8684H2/H4 and ESP8684-MINI-1-H4.

mcus.name: ESP32-C3
mcus.description: Low-cost 160 MHz RISC-V Wi-Fi + BLE 5 SoC with built-in USB serial/JTAG; the cheap, easy default for small connected sensors and controllers.
notes: Native USB is a fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller (CDC-ACM + JTAG): great for flashing/debugging, but no HID/MSC or custom USB devices.
Strapping pins GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9; GPIO18/19 are the USB D-/D+ pins.
Bare ESP32-C3 needs external QSPI flash; all variants need a 40 MHz crystal and RF matching.
Espressif now recommends the 'X' (chip v1.1) parts for new designs: ESP32-C3FH4X (only 16 GPIO) / FH8X and ESP32-C3-MINI-1-N4X/H4X (the plain MINI-1-N4 is NRND).
ADC2 is unreliable on early revisions; use ADC1 channels (GPIO0-4).

mcus.name: ESP32-C5
mcus.description: 240 MHz RISC-V SoC with dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 6, BLE, Thread/Zigbee and two CAN-FD controllers; pick it when 2.4 GHz is congested or you need 5 GHz.
mcus.core: RISC-V 32-bit (RV32IMAC) HP core + 48 MHz LP RISC-V core
notes: Only Espressif SoC with 5 GHz Wi-Fi (dual-band Wi-Fi 6); BLE is certified to Bluetooth Core 6.0.
Two CAN-FD controllers (ISO 11898-1:2015) - need external transceivers.
Needs a 48 MHz crystal. ESP32-C5HR8/HR2 have in-package PSRAM only and still need external flash.
USB is the fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller (no HID/MSC).
PlatformIO support is via the community pioarduino platform.
Datasheet EP is 4.7 mm; the nearest KiCad footprint uses a 4.66 mm pad (within tolerance).

mcus.name: ESP32-C6
mcus.description: 160 MHz RISC-V SoC with Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5.3 and 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee) plus a low-power core; a cheap all-in-one choice for Matter devices and border routers.
mcus.core: RISC-V 32-bit (RV32IMAC) HP core + 20 MHz LP RISC-V core
notes: Wi-Fi, BLE and 802.15.4 share one 2.4 GHz radio (time-division coexistence).
USB is the fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller (no HID/MSC). SDIO is slave-only (no SD-card host).
Counts include the LP UART and LP I2C. Two classic CAN 2.0 (TWAI) controllers.
QFN40 ESP32-C6 needs external flash; ESP32-C6FH4/FH8 (QFN32) have in-package flash but only 22 GPIO. 40 MHz crystal required.
Strapping pins GPIO4 (MTMS), GPIO5 (MTDI), GPIO8, GPIO9 and GPIO15; GPIO12/13 are USB D-/D+.

mcus.name: ESP32-C61
mcus.description: Cost-optimised 160 MHz RISC-V Wi-Fi 6 + BLE SoC that adds PSRAM support; a Wi-Fi 6 upgrade path from the ESP32-C3 for memory-hungrier apps.
notes: No 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee) and no CAN, unlike the ESP32-C6; BLE certified to Core 6.0.
PSRAM is in-package only (HR2/HR8); HR variants need external flash, HF4 has no PSRAM.
USB is the fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller (no HID/MSC); SDIO is slave-only.
Arduino-ESP32 supports the C61 only as an ESP-IDF component / custom lib build; MicroPython has no C61 port yet.
Needs a 40 MHz crystal.

mcus.name: ESP32-H2
mcus.description: 96 MHz RISC-V SoC with BLE 5.3 and 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee) but no Wi-Fi; low-power choice for battery Matter-over-Thread and Zigbee end devices.
notes: No Wi-Fi: Matter-over-Thread end devices need a Thread border router (e.g. ESP32-C6/S3 + H2).
Flash is in-package only (2 or 4 MB); the flash pins are not routed out, so no external flash or PSRAM.
Needs a 32 MHz crystal. USB is the fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller. Strapping pins GPIO8, GPIO9 and GPIO25.
Current datasheet lists the 'S' revisions (ESP32-H2FH2S/FH4S, MINI-1-H2S/H4S); the original FH4 is still widely stocked.

mcus.name: ESP32-P4
mcus.description: 400 MHz dual-core RISC-V application MCU (no radio) with up to 32 MB in-package PSRAM, MIPI-DSI/CSI, H.264/JPEG, USB 2.0 High-Speed and Ethernet for HMI and camera products.
mcus.core: RISC-V 32-bit dual-core HP (RV32IMAFC + AI/SIMD extensions) + 40 MHz LP RISC-V core
notes: No Wi-Fi/Bluetooth: pair with an ESP32-C6/C5 over SDIO (ESP-Hosted) for wireless.
Requires external QSPI flash (up to 64 MB) and a 40 MHz crystal; PSRAM is 1.8 V in-package.
USB: one High-Speed OTG with internal PHY plus one Full-Speed OTG; a separate USB Serial/JTAG controller is also available.
Counts include LP peripherals (LP UART, LP I2C, LP SPI); I3C and the analog I2C are not counted. Three classic CAN 2.0 (TWAI) controllers.
Use the 'X' parts (chip revision v3.x, 400 MHz); earlier v1.x silicon (no X suffix) is slower and unsupported by esp-hal. Datasheet is still pre-release.
No KiCad library footprint for the QFN-104 (0.35 mm pitch, 7.5 mm EP).

mcus.name: ESP8266EX
mcus.description: The original ultra-cheap Wi-Fi MCU; still fine for simple Arduino Wi-Fi projects via ESP-12F modules, but legacy (NRND) with few hardware peripherals.
notes: Marked NRND by Espressif; the ESP32-C2/C3 are the suggested replacements.
I2C and PWM are software-implemented (any GPIO via Arduino Wire/analogWrite) - counted as 0 hardware channels here.
UART1 is TX-only (typically used for logs). ADC is a single 10-bit input (0-1 V on the bare chip).
RAM: 80 KB data RAM + 32 KB IRAM; only ~50 KB heap is left with Wi-Fi connected.
Strapping pins GPIO0, GPIO2 and GPIO15; deep-sleep wake needs GPIO16 tied to RST. Needs a USB-UART bridge to flash.
Bare chip needs external SPI flash, a 26/40 MHz crystal and RF matching; ESP-12F is the usual module (Ai-Thinker).
I2C and PWM are implemented in software (Arduino Wire / analogWrite work fine); counted here as 1 I2C bus and 4 PWM outputs.

mcus.name: GD32F303
mcus.description: 120 MHz Cortex-M4F STM32F103/F303-style workhorse with up to 1 MB flash, USB FS device, CAN, SDIO and 5 UARTs; cheap and widely stocked.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: GD32F30x Firmware Library (GD32 Embedded Builder / Keil / IAR)

notes: Only the first 256 KB of flash is zero-wait ('code area'); the rest ('data area') runs much slower, so keep hot code in the first 256 KB.
USB is full-speed device only (USBD), no host. 48-pin parts have 3 USARTs, 10 ADC channels and no SDIO; UART3/4 and SDIO need LQFP-64+, EXMC (8080 LCD/SRAM) needs LQFP-100+.
Largely pin-compatible with STM32F103; ST HAL/STM32duino code often runs with tweaks (faster clocks, different flash timing). Use GigaDevice's firmware library for full support.
ROM bootloader over USART0 (PA9/PA10) via BOOT0; standard Arm SWD/JTAG probes work.
128 KB 'xB' parts (e.g. GD32F303CBT6) have a separate datasheet.

mcus.name: GD32VF103
mcus.description: Early mainstream RISC-V MCU (Longan Nano): 108 MHz, 128 KB flash, USB FS OTG with ROM DFU bootloader, 2x CAN and 5 UARTs in an STM32F103-like layout.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: Nuclei SDK / GD32VF103 Firmware Library (Nuclei Studio)

notes: Out of stock at LCSC/JLCPCB when checked (Nov 2026) and pricey for what it is; CH32V203/CH32V307 are cheaper RISC-V alternatives with similar peripherals.
ROM bootloader supports USB DFU (no programmer needed) plus USART0/USART1. Debug is RISC-V JTAG (e.g. Sipeed RV-Debugger, J-Link, FT2232).
Small packages lose peripherals: CB has 3 UARTs; TB (QFN-36) has 2 UARTs, 1 I2C, 1 SPI. EXMC only on LQFP-100.
Rust: gd32vf103xx-hal / longan-nano crates. PlatformIO 'gd32v' platform (Sipeed) also offers a basic Arduino framework.

mcus.name: GD32E230
mcus.description: Low-cost 72 MHz Cortex-M23 with up to 64 KB flash, 2 USART/I2C/SPI and 1.8-3.6 V supply; an inexpensive STM32F030/G030-class part from about $0.40.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: GD32E23x Firmware Library (GD32 Embedded Builder / Keil / IAR)

notes: No USB, no CAN. The x8 (64 KB) parts get a 2nd I2C, 2nd SPI and an extra timer; x4 parts have 1 USART.
Cortex-M23 (Armv8-M Baseline) rather than M0+, so check toolchain/RTOS support; also offered in a tiny 3x3 mm LGA-20.
ROM bootloader on USART0 (PA9/PA10) or USART1 (PA14/PA15) via BOOT0; standard Arm SWD probes work.

mcus.name: HPM5361
mcus.description: 480 MHz RISC-V MCU with 1 MB in-package flash, 4x CAN-FD, high-speed USB with built-in PHY and motor-control timers in QFN-48/LQFP; a cheap, fast pick for CAN-FD + USB designs.
notes: CAN: 4x Bosch M_CAN (MCAN) controllers, all CAN-FD (up to 8 Mbit/s), plus 4x LIN. All four CAN ports can be pinned out even on the QFN-48. HPM5321 has the same CAN/UART set without the motor-control blocks; HPM5331/HPM5301 have no CAN.
USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG with integrated HS PHY. On LQFP-64/QFN-48 USB_DP/DM share pins PA24/PA25 (set them to analog mode for USB).

The 1 MB flash is in-package (stacked serial NOR on XPI0) and is the boot device. XPI0 port-A pins are also brought out (datasheet lists Quad SPI NOR/PSRAM/HyperRAM support), but external flash/PSRAM is not counted here.
ROM ISP: UART0 on every package, but USB ISP only on the LQFP-100 (LQFP-64/QFN-48 boot ROM is UART0-only). Boot mode set by pins PA02/PA03. Debug is JTAG.
No SD/SDIO host, Ethernet or I2S: use SPI for microSD.
QFN-48 drops UART4/UART5 and SPI3 (7 UART, 3 SPI); LQFP-64 drops UART4/UART5.
Single 3.0-3.6 V supply; on-chip DCDC (needs an inductor) makes the 1.1-1.3 V core rail. IO banks run at 3.3 V or 1.8 V.
No battery-backed RTC or 32.768 kHz crystal input (only an internal 32 kHz RC). Shutdown current is about 2.3 uA, but SRAM is not retained.
Power: about 33.5 mA from 3.3 V at 480 MHz running CoreMark from ILM with peripherals off (about 60 mA with all peripherals on).

Software: HPM SDK (GCC/CMake, free SEGGER Embedded Studio) and RT-Thread BSPs. Not in upstream Zephyr (HPMicro maintains its own fork). The hpm-hal Rust crate (embassy) exists but is marked work-in-progress.

mcus.name: HPM6750
mcus.description: Dual 816 MHz RISC-V MCU with 2 MB SRAM, 4x CAN-FD, two High-Speed USB OTG with PHYs, two gigabit Ethernet MACs, two SD/eMMC hosts, SDRAM, LCD and camera; MPU-class I/O without Linux.
notes: CAN: 4x CAN-FD controllers (up to 8 Mbit/s). These are HPMicro's own CAN IP, not the Bosch M_CAN used on HPM5300/HPM6200, so the drivers differ. The HPM6730 is the CAN 2.0-only sibling.
2x USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG, each with its own integrated HS PHY.
Flashless: boots from external serial NOR on XPI0/XPI1 (Quad/Octal SPI, HyperFlash; 255 MB memory-mapped window per XPI). The HPM6754 is the variant with 4 MB in-package flash.

External RAM: the FEMC SDRAM controller (8/16/32-bit, 166 MHz, 256 MB window) is the usual choice. The XPIs also support Quad/Octal SPI PSRAM and HyperRAM; psramMaxMB 64 assumes the largest common OPI PSRAM/HyperRAM part.
Ethernet: 2x 10/100/1000 MACs with RGMII/RMII (external PHY needed), IEEE 1588 timestamps.
The BGA-196 (IAN) is cut down: 125 GPIO, 18 analog inputs, 1 SD/eMMC (SDXC0), 16-bit SDRAM only, ENET1 limited to 100 Mbit, and XPI0 brought out only on its CB port (boot flash must go there).
ROM serial boot/ISP over UART0 or USB0 (USB-HID), selected by BOOT_MODE pins PZ06/PZ07. Debug is JTAG.
Single 3.0-3.6 V supply; on-chip DCDC makes the 1.275 V core rail. IO banks run at 3.3 V or 1.8 V. Separate VBAT (2.4-3.6 V) for the RTC/battery domain draws about 5.5 uA in shutdown.
Power: about 128 mA from 3.3 V at 816 MHz on one core with peripherals off, and about 330 mA with both cores and all peripherals on. Plan for heat.

Software: HPM SDK (GCC/CMake, free SEGGER Embedded Studio) and RT-Thread BSPs. Not in upstream Zephyr (HPMicro maintains its own fork). The hpm-hal Rust crate (embassy) exists but is marked work-in-progress.

mcus.name: HPM6280
mcus.description: Dual 600 MHz RISC-V MCU with 800 KB SRAM, 4x CAN-FD, High-Speed USB with PHY, 100 ps high-resolution PWM and 16-bit ADCs; aimed at digital power and motor control.
notes: CAN: 4x Bosch M_CAN (MCAN) controllers, all CAN-FD (up to 8 Mbit/s), plus 4x LIN. All four are available on every package.
1x USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG with integrated HS PHY.
No SD/SDIO host, Ethernet or I2S: use SPI for microSD.

Flashless: boots from external serial NOR on the single XPI0 (256 MB window; Quad/Octal SPI). The HPM6284 is the variant with 4 MB in-package flash. The XPI also supports PSRAM/HyperRAM, but it shares the one controller with the boot flash, so psramMaxMB is left at 0.

The '-PA' package is an eLQFP-144: its bottom exposed pad is VSS and must be soldered. The datasheet gives two lead-frame options (EP 5.0 mm or 9.74 mm); 5 x 5 mm is listed here as the safe land size. Confirm with HPMicro before layout.

Motor/power control: 2x 8-ch high-resolution PWM (100 ps), 2x 8-ch PWM (3 ns), 4x QEI/Hall, 2 programmable logic arrays (PLA) and a sigma-delta filter (SDM). DAC outputs are only on the LQFP-144; the BGA-116 and eLQFP-100 have 73 GPIO and 15 analog inputs.
ROM serial boot/ISP over UART0 or USB0 (USB-HID), selected by BOOT_MODE pins PA20/PA21. Debug is JTAG.
Single 3.0-3.6 V supply; on-chip DCDC makes the core rail. IO banks run at 3.3 V or 1.8 V. VBAT (2.4-3.6 V) powers the RTC domain at about 1.6 uA.
Power: about 84 mA from 3.3 V at 600 MHz on one core with peripherals off, and about 155 mA on both cores. Stop mode still draws a few mA.

Software: HPM SDK (GCC/CMake, free SEGGER Embedded Studio) and RT-Thread BSPs. Not in upstream Zephyr (HPMicro maintains its own fork). The hpm-hal Rust crate (embassy) exists but is marked work-in-progress.

mcus.name: PSoC 62 (CY8C62xx)
mcus.description: Dual-core 150 MHz Cortex-M4F + Cortex-M0+ with up to 2 MB flash / 1 MB SRAM, CapSense touch, USB FS, SD host, QSPI XIP and crypto; a low-power, touch-capable MCU for IoT. It has no radio.
notes: No radio. PSoC 63 is the BLE line, and Infineon's Wi-Fi/BT kits pair a PSoC 62 with an external CYW43xxx combo chip.

Serial ports come from SCBs that are each UART, SPI or I2C at runtime, so the uart/i2c/spi counts are per-type maxima, not additive. CY8C62x8/xA has 13 SCBs: 8 UART/SPI/I2C, 4 UART/I2C only, and 1 Deep Sleep SPI/I2C. CY8C62x7 has 9 SCBs (8 + 1 Deep Sleep) and CY8C62x5 has 7 (6 + 1 Deep Sleep).

Peripherals differ by sub-line. CAN FD (1 block) exists only on CY8C62x5 (-S3D6x/-S3D7x parts). SD host: 2 on CY8C62x8/xA, 1 on 62x5, none on 62x7. I2S: 2 on 62x8/xA, 1 on 62x7, none on 62x5. The 12-bit DAC, 2 opamps and 12 UDBs are only on CY8C62x7.
USB is full-speed device/host only, with no high-speed PHY.
UDBs (62x7 only) and Smart I/O give some programmable logic, but they are not comparable to RP2040 PIO.
There is no ROM UART/USB bootloader, so blank chips must be flashed over SWD (KitProg3, MiniProg4 or J-Link). DFU/MCUboot can be added in firmware.
The Infineon Arduino core (arduino-core-psoc6) only supports the CY8CKIT-062S2-AI board (CY8C624ABZI-S2D44). Infineon's MicroPython port for PSoC 6 lives in Infineon's fork, not upstream MicroPython.
activeUaPerMhz is the CM4 at 1.1 V core (LP mode, needed for 150 MHz). The 0.9 V ULP mode (up to 50 MHz) gives 22-27 uA/MHz.
CapSense works on any GPIO except the dedicated CMOD capacitor pin, so touchChannels is the GPIO count minus one.
SMIF supports single, dual and quad SPI (octal and dual-quad on 62x7/62x8/62xA) with XIP and on-the-fly AES. externalFlashMaxMB assumes the 128 MB XIP window.

mcus.name: PSoC 4100S / 4100S Plus
mcus.description: 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with best-in-class CapSense touch, opamps and a 12-bit SAR ADC, running from 1.71-5.5 V. The 4100S Plus adds 128 KB flash, 5 serial blocks and classic CAN.
notes: Serial ports come from SCBs that are each I2C, SPI or UART at runtime: 5 on the 4100S Plus, 3 on the 4100S. The uart/i2c/spi counts are per-type maxima and share the same blocks.

CAN is classic CAN 2.0B (no FD) and only on 4100S Plus parts with a 6 or 7 in the suffix (e.g. -S465, -S475). CapSense needs a 5 or 7 there (e.g. -S455, -S475), and plain 4100S parts with -S43x have CapSense.
Runs directly from 1.71-5.5 V, so 5 V systems need no regulator.
There is no hardware calendar RTC. The WCO 32 kHz crystal plus watchdog counters are used for timekeeping in firmware.
The two 7-bit IDACs are current DACs, mainly for CapSense, and there is no voltage DAC. Also on chip: 2 opamps (CTBm), 2 low-power comparators and Smart I/O logic (no UDBs).
The 4100S Plus has a TRNG but no crypto accelerator.
There is no ROM bootloader, so blank chips are programmed over SWD (KitProg3/MiniProg4). A bootloader can be added in firmware.
CapSense works on any GPIO except the CMOD capacitor pin, so touchChannels is the GPIO count minus one.
The SAR ADC sequencer has 16 single-ended channels via the AMUX bus. The 4100S (non-Plus) has 64 KB flash, 8 KB SRAM, 5 TCPWMs and up to 36 GPIO.
The larger PSoC 4100S Plus 256 KB (CY8C4148) and 4100S Max (CY8C4149) are separate lines and are not included here.

mcus.name: XMC1100
mcus.description: Cheap 32 MHz Cortex-M0 in a hand-solderable TSSOP-38 that runs from 1.8-5.5 V, with a 12-bit ADC, RTC and two flexible USIC serial channels. A good 8-bit replacement.
notes: There are two USIC channels (USIC0 CH0/CH1). Each one is UART, SPI (also dual/quad SPI), I2C, I2S or LIN, so the uart/i2c/spi/i2s counts share the same 2 channels.
The CPU runs at 32 MHz while peripherals (PCLK) can run at 64 MHz. There is no FPU, MATH coprocessor, CAN, USB or DAC (those come with XMC1300/1400).
Only one CCU4 timer unit, so there are just 4 PWM outputs. LED/touch (LEDTS), BCCU and CCU8 are on XMC1200/1300, not the XMC1100.
ADC: 12 channels on TSSOP-38/VQFN-40, 8 on VQFN-24 and 6 on TSSOP-16. On TSSOP-38, 8 of the 34 port pins (P2.2-P2.9) are input-only analog/digital.

Devices ship in ASC (UART) bootstrap-loader mode via USIC0. Code is loaded to SRAM, so flashing needs a loader tool (e.g. XMC Flasher/DAVE), and the Boot Mode Index (BMI) must then be switched to a user mode. SWD or single-pin SPD debug works too.
The 128/200 KB versions (XMC1100-T038X0128/X0200) exist but are rarely stocked. flashKB reflects the 64 KB parts listed.
deepSleepUa is the datasheet deep-sleep figure (0.24 mA at 5 V, flash off). There is no hibernate mode, so this is not a coin-cell part.
USIC quad-SPI is a protocol mode, not a memory-mapped flash interface, so qspi is false.
Arduino support is the XMC-for-Arduino core (KIT_XMC11_BOOT_001 board); the PlatformIO platform is Infineon's infineonxmc.

mcus.name: XMC4700
mcus.description: 144 MHz Cortex-M4F industrial MCU with 2 MB flash, 352 KB SRAM, Ethernet, USB OTG, SD/MMC, six classic CAN nodes and rich motor-control timers. Good for gateways, PLC-style I/O and drives.
notes: MultiCAN has 6 nodes and 256 message objects but is classic CAN 2.0B only (up to 1 Mbit/s). There is no CAN FD.
There are 6 USIC channels (3 modules x 2). Each one is UART, SPI (dual/quad), I2C, I2S or LIN, so the uart/i2c/spi/i2s counts all share these 6 channels.

USB is 2.0 full-speed OTG with an integrated PHY (no high-speed). The Ethernet 10/100 MAC uses MII/RMII on LQFP-144 and RMII only on LQFP-100. The XMC4800 is the same chip plus an EtherCAT slave controller.
The EBU external bus (SDRAM, NOR, SRAM; 16-bit muxed only on LQFP-100) can also drive 8080-style LCD modules. There is no QSPI flash controller; USIC quad-SPI is not memory-mapped.

pwmChannels counts 16 CCU4 slices plus 8 CCU8 slices x 2 compare channels (CCU8 also gives complementary outputs with dead time). There are also 2 POSIF encoder/hall interfaces and a 4-channel delta-sigma demodulator.
The LQFP-100 version has 24 ADC channels and 75 I/O. LQFP-144 has 32 ADC channels and 119 I/O, of which 26 (ports 14/15) are input-only analog/digital.

Both LQFP packages have an exposed die pad (7.0 x 7.0 mm incl. U-groove, 6.2 mm without) that must be soldered to VSS. The KiCad 1EP footprints listed are the closest library match; check them against Infineon's land pattern.
deepSleepUa is hibernate with the RTC running (VBAT 3.3 V), where SRAM is lost. Deep sleep with SRAM retention draws about 7 mA.
Supply is 3.3 V only (3.13-3.63 V).
ROM bootstrap loaders: ASC (UART) and CAN BSL, selected by the TCK/TMS levels at reset.
Arduino support is the XMC-for-Arduino core (KIT_XMC47_RELAX board); Zephyr has the xmc47_relax_kit board.

mcus.name: ATmega328P
mcus.description: The Arduino Uno chip: a breadboard-friendly 8-bit AVR in DIP-28 that runs straight from 5 V, with a huge library ecosystem and dead-simple hardware.
notes: Blank chips have no bootloader: burn the Arduino (Optiboot) bootloader once with an ISP programmer (or another Arduino as ISP), then upload over a USB-serial adapter.
20 MHz needs 4.5-5.5 V; at 3.3 V stay at or below ~13 MHz (8 MHz internal RC is common).
ADC6/ADC7 (analog-only) exist only on the TQFP/QFN packages; DIP-28 has 6 ADC inputs.
The USART can also act as a second SPI master (MSPIM).
RTC = Timer2 asynchronous 'real-time counter' with a 32.768 kHz crystal on the XTAL pins (then the core must run from the internal RC).
The ATmega328PB (TQFP/QFN only) adds a 2nd USART, SPI and I2C, but is not a drop-in replacement (former VCC/GND pins become GPIO).

mcus.name: ATmega32U4
mcus.description: 8-bit AVR with native full-speed USB device (Arduino Leonardo / Pro Micro): great for USB keyboards, MIDI and HID gadgets at 5 V.
notes: Crystal versions (-AU/-MU) ship with Atmel's USB DFU bootloader pre-programmed in the boot section (flash, not ROM): flash with dfu-programmer / FLIP without a programmer. The RC-oscillator ATmega32U4RC parts ship blank.
The Arduino 'Caterina' bootloader is not pre-installed; burn it via ISP if you want Arduino IDE uploads.
2.5 KB SRAM (ramKB rounds down to 2). USB is device-only (no host); 16 MHz operation needs 4.5-5.5 V (8 MHz at 3.3 V).
Needs a 16 MHz (or 8 MHz) crystal and a 1 uF UCAP capacitor for the internal USB regulator.

mcus.name: ATmega2560
mcus.description: The Arduino Mega chip: 86 I/O, 4 hardware serial ports and 256 KB flash in a 5 V 8-bit AVR, ideal for pin-hungry 3D printers and controllers.
notes: 16 MHz requires 4.5-5.5 V (8 MHz from 2.7 V); the ATmega2560V runs from 1.8 V at lower clocks.
Blank chips need an ISP programmer to install the Arduino (stk500v2) bootloader.
Only offered in TQFP-100 (0.5 mm pitch) and BGA: not breadboard-friendly; relatively expensive for an 8-bit MCU.
RTC = asynchronous Timer2 with a 32.768 kHz crystal on TOSC pins.

mcus.name: ATmega4809
mcus.description: Modern 5 V megaAVR (Arduino Nano Every / Uno WiFi Rev2) with 4 USARTs, 48 KB flash, an RTC and simple 1-wire UPDI programming.
notes: Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.
The DIP-40 version uses the 48-pin die with fewer pads bonded (33 I/O); unbonded pins PB[5:0]/PC[7:6] must be configured (pull-up or input-disable).
Not register-compatible with the ATmega328P: Arduino code works through the megaAVR core / MegaCoreX, but direct port/register code must be ported.
Has an internal 16/20 MHz oscillator, so no crystal is needed.

mcus.name: ATtiny85
mcus.description: Classic 8-pin DIP/SOIC AVR (Digispark, Adafruit Trinket): tiny 5 V jobs like LED drivers, sensors and simple controllers with Arduino support.
notes: Only 512 bytes of SRAM (ramKB rounds to 0).
No hardware UART; I2C and SPI share the single USI (Universal Serial Interface), which needs software assistance - use one at a time.
6 I/O only if RESET is disabled as GPIO (then high-voltage programming is needed to reflash); 5 I/O normally.
Blank chips need an ISP programmer; the -20 grade runs 2.7-5.5 V (ATtiny85V: 1.8 V at up to 10 MHz).
The SOIC is the 208-mil (5.3 mm) wide-body version, not standard 150-mil SOIC-8.
For new designs the ATtiny412 / ATtiny202 (tinyAVR 1/0-series) are cheaper and add a real USART.

mcus.name: ATtiny412
mcus.description: Tiny, cheap 8-pin SOIC AVR with a real USART, I2C, SPI, DAC and event system; runs at 5 V and programs over a single UPDI wire.
notes: Only 256 bytes of SRAM and 4 KB flash (ramKB rounds to 0).
6 GPIO counts the UPDI/RESET pin; using it as GPIO makes reprogramming need a 12 V UPDI high-voltage programmer, so plan on 5 usable I/O.
DAC is 8-bit, one output. USART, I2C and SPI pins overlap heavily on 8 pins - check the mux table.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.
Arduino support via the community megaTinyCore.

mcus.name: ATtiny1616
mcus.description: 20-pin 5 V tinyAVR with 16 KB flash, two ADCs, a DAC and 12-channel hardware capacitive touch (PTC); cheap and UPDI-programmable.
notes: Two 10-bit ADCs (ADC0: 12 inputs, ADC1: 8 inputs, sharing pins); the PTC takes over ADC0 while touch is active.
Three 8-bit DACs, but only DAC0 has a pin output (the others feed the analog comparators).
PTC: 12 self-capacitance or 36 mutual-capacitance touch channels (QTouch library).
The SOIC-20 is the 300-mil wide-body package.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.

mcus.name: ATtiny3224
mcus.description: 14-pin 5 V tinyAVR with 32 KB flash, two USARTs and a 12-bit differential ADC with programmable gain - great for small sensor front-ends.
notes: Unlike the 1-series it has no DAC, no TCD and no touch (PTC), but gets a second USART and a 12-bit differential ADC with 1-16x PGA.
12 GPIO counts the UPDI/RESET pin.
Pin-compatible 20/24-pin siblings: ATtiny3226 / ATtiny3227.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.

mcus.name: AVR128DA
mcus.description: Biggest modern 5 V AVR: 128 KB flash, 16 KB RAM, up to 6 USARTs, 12-bit ADC, DAC and hardware touch, with DIP-28 to TQFP-64 options.
notes: Peripheral counts scale with pin count: USART 3/3/5/6, I2C 1/2/2/2, ADC inputs 10/14/18/22, PTC self-cap channels 18/22/32/46 for 28/32/48/64 pins.
GPIO counts include the input-only PF6/RESET pin.
Internal 24 MHz oscillator with auto-tune from a 32 kHz crystal; no crystal needed.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.
Arduino support via the community DxCore.

mcus.name: AVR128DB
mcus.description: 5 V AVR with multi-voltage I/O (talk to 1.8/3.3 V parts on one port), built-in op-amps and a crystal oscillator - good for mixed-signal and level-shifting jobs.
notes: MVIO: PORTC runs from a separate VDDIO2 rail (1.8-5.5 V) for built-in level shifting.
2 op-amps (28/32-pin) or 3 op-amps (48/64-pin); no PTC touch controller (unlike AVR DA).
Peripheral counts scale with pin count: USART 3/3/5/6, I2C 1/2/2/2, ADC inputs 9/13/18/22 for 28/32/48/64 pins.
GPIO counts include the input-only PF6/RESET pin.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.
Arduino support via the community DxCore.

mcus.name: AVR64DD
mcus.description: Low-cost 5 V AVR from 14 to 32 pins with multi-voltage I/O, 12-bit ADC and DAC; a modern, cheap replacement for ATmega328-class designs.
notes: MVIO: PORTC can run from a separate VDDIO2 rail (1.8-5.5 V) for level shifting.
ADC inputs scale with pins: 7/13/19/23 for 14/20/28/32 pins. GPIO counts include the input-only PF6/RESET pin.
The 14/20-pin parts are covered by a separate data sheet (AVR64DD14/20).
No official KiCad symbol yet.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.
Arduino support via the community DxCore.

mcus.name: AVR64EA
mcus.description: 5 V AVR focused on precision analog: 12-bit differential ADC with programmable gain, 10-bit DAC and very low 0.08 uA power-down current.
notes: ADC: 12-bit differential with 1-16x PGA and hardware accumulation for 17-bit oversampled results; ADC inputs 20/24/28 for 28/32/48 pins.
Two TCA + four TCB timers; no TCD, no PTC, no MVIO. Max 20 MHz.
GPIO counts include the input-only PF6/RESET pin.
Arduino/PlatformIO community support is limited compared with AVR DA/DB/DD (DxCore); plan on MPLAB X / AVR-GCC.
Blank chips are flashed over the 1-wire UPDI pin; a USB-serial adapter plus a resistor (SerialUPDI) or any cheap UPDI programmer works.

mcus.name: ATSAMD21
mcus.description: The Arduino Zero / Adafruit M0 chip: a cheap 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with native USB, six flexible SERCOM serial ports and excellent CircuitPython support.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). SERCOMs: 4 on E (32-pin), 6 on G/J.
ADC inputs 10/14/20 and PTC self-cap touch channels 6/10/16 (up to 256 mutual-cap) for E/G/J packages.
USB full-speed device + embedded host; can run crystal-less from the internal 48 MHz DFLL locked to USB SOF.
No FPU and only 32 KB RAM: fine for CircuitPython/Arduino, tight for big buffers.

mcus.name: ATSAMD51
mcus.description: 120 MHz Cortex-M4F with FPU, 1 MB flash, 256 KB RAM, native USB, QSPI and SD host: the Adafruit M4 chip, great for CircuitPython, audio and displays.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
External QSPI flash is memory-mapped (XIP) in a 16 MB window; 8 KB backup SRAM survives Backup mode.
Active current ~65 uA/MHz with the internal buck regulator (~137 uA/MHz on the default LDO).

uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). 6 SERCOMs on G/J, 8 on the 100/128-pin N/P parts (not listed here).
G (48-pin) parts lose I2S and have 20 ADC inputs; J has 24. PCC = 10-bit parallel capture (camera) on G/J.
Crypto: AES, TRNG, public-key accelerator (PUKCC) and SHA via ICM.

mcus.name: ATSAME51
mcus.description: SAMD51 plus two CAN-FD controllers: a 120 MHz Cortex-M4F with USB, QSPI and SD host for CAN-connected robots, vehicles and industrial nodes.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
External QSPI flash is memory-mapped (XIP) in a 16 MB window; 8 KB backup SRAM survives Backup mode.
Active current ~65 uA/MHz with the internal buck regulator (~137 uA/MHz on the default LDO).
CAN-FD (ISO 11898-1:2015) x2 on J/N packages; the 48-pin G package has only one CAN. External CAN transceiver required.
uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). 6 SERCOMs on J (64-pin), 8 on N (100-pin).
The data sheet table lists 1 SDHC on SAME51N (vs 2 on SAMD51N/SAME54N); treat a second SD host as unavailable.
Used on the Adafruit Feather M4 CAN (Arduino + CircuitPython).

mcus.name: ATSAME54
mcus.description: 120 MHz Cortex-M4F with 10/100 Ethernet MAC, two CAN-FD, USB, QSPI and two SD hosts - a single-chip gateway for Ethernet + CAN industrial designs.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
External QSPI flash is memory-mapped (XIP) in a 16 MB window; 8 KB backup SRAM survives Backup mode.
Active current ~65 uA/MHz with the internal buck regulator (~137 uA/MHz on the default LDO).
Ethernet MAC (MII/RMII) needs an external PHY (e.g. KSZ8091/LAN8720).
SAME54 starts at 100 pins (N = TQFP-100, P = TQFP-128 / 0.4 mm pitch); ADC inputs 28 (N) / 32 (P).
uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). 8 SERCOMs on N/P.
Popular dev board: SAM E54 Xplained Pro (Zephyr, CircuitPython, Harmony).

mcus.name: ATSAME70
mcus.description: 300 MHz Cortex-M7 with double-precision FPU, 2 MB flash, High-Speed USB with on-chip PHY, Ethernet, two CAN-FD and a camera interface.
notes: SAM-BA bootloader in ROM over UART0 or USB (USB boot needs a 12 or 16 MHz crystal); an erased part boots SAM-BA. Assert the ERASE pin to get back to it.
Order revision B parts (…B-AN): CAN-FD is ISO 11898-1:2015 compliant on rev B. KiCad only has symbols for the legacy rev A (ATSAME70x21A-AN, same pinout).
The 64-pin ATSAME70J has no USB, only one CAN, 5 ADC inputs and no SD/MMC; the N (100-pin) has 1 SPI, 1 I2SC and 10 ADC inputs.
uart = 3 USART + 5 UART; i2s = SSC + 2 I2SC. LCD = 8080-style module via the 16-bit SMC (no RGB controller).
USB High-Speed needs VDDIO >= 3.0 V. Ethernet MAC (MII/RMII) needs an external PHY.

mcus.name: ATSAMC21
mcus.description: 5 V-capable 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with two CAN-FD controllers, a 16-bit sigma-delta ADC and touch - built for robust 5 V automotive and industrial nodes.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
CAN-FD: 1 on E (32-pin), 2 on G/J/N. External CAN transceiver required.
uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). SERCOMs: 4/6/6/8 on E/G/J/N.
Two 12-bit ADCs (unique inputs 10/14/20/22 for E/G/J/N) plus a 16-bit sigma-delta ADC (1/2/3 differential channels).
No USB. 48 MHz up to 125 C; '64' ordering-suffix parts run 64 MHz up to 85 C.
No official KiCad symbol.

mcus.name: ATSAML21
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ (~40 uA/MHz, sub-uA backup) with USB, AES, 12-bit DAC and op-amps for battery-powered sensors.
notes: No ROM bootloader: blank chips must be flashed once over SWD (e.g. to install an Arduino/UF2 bootloader); afterwards USB uploads work.
ramKB = 32 KB SRAM + 8 KB low-power SRAM.
Backup mode 0.64 uA with RTC; Standby with RTC and full RAM retention ~1.4 uA. ~40 uA/MHz needs the internal buck regulator (77-95 uA/MHz on LDO).

uart/i2c/spi counts are SERCOMs: each SERCOM is either a USART, I2C or SPI, so the totals are shared (e.g. 6 SERCOMs = 3 UART + 2 I2C + 1 SPI). 6 SERCOMs on all packages (one sits in the low-power domain).
3 op-amps, 2 comparators, AES-256 and TRNG. ADC inputs 10/14/20 and PTC self-cap channels 7/10/16 for E/G/J.
Order revision B parts (...B-...); revision A was engineering samples only.

mcus.name: PIC16F18446
mcus.description: Low-cost 5 V 8-bit PIC in DIP/SOIC/SSOP-20 with a 12-bit computing ADC, CLCs and core-independent peripherals for simple analog and control tasks.
notes: Blank chips need an ICSP programmer/debugger (PICkit 4/5, MPLAB Snap or ICD); there is no factory bootloader.
32 MHz clock = 8 MIPS (4 clocks per instruction).
1 EUSART; the 2 MSSP modules are each either I2C or SPI (i2c/spi counts are shared).
PWM = 4 CCP + 2 dedicated 10-bit PWM; also 2 CWG, 4 CLC, NCO, 24-bit SMT. DAC is only 5-bit.
Touch = capacitive voltage divider (CVD) sensing in hardware on the ADC2 inputs (mTouch library), not a dedicated touch controller.
One of the 18 I/O (MCLR/RA3) is input-only. The PIC16LF18446 variant runs 1.8-3.6 V.

mcus.name: PIC18F-Q84
mcus.description: 5 V 8-bit PIC with a built-in CAN FD controller, 5 UARTs, DMA and a 12-bit computing ADC; offered in hobbyist-friendly DIP-28/DIP-40.
notes: Blank chips need an ICSP programmer/debugger (PICkit 4/5, MPLAB Snap or ICD); there is no factory bootloader.
64 MHz clock = 16 MIPS. SRAM is 12.8 KB (ramKB rounds down); 1 KB EEPROM; 8-channel DMA.
One CAN FD controller (also CAN 2.0B); needs an external CAN FD transceiver.
ADC inputs 24/35/43 for 28/40-44/48-pin parts; hardware CVD touch on ADC inputs (mTouch), not a dedicated touch controller.
PWM = 4 x 16-bit dual-output PWM (8 outputs) + 3 CCP; also 8 CLC, 3 NCO, 3 CWG. DAC is 8-bit.
UARTs support LIN, DMX and DALI in hardware.

mcus.name: dsPIC33CK256MP50x
mcus.description: 100 MIPS 16-bit DSC with CAN FD, 250 ps high-resolution PWM, three fast 12-bit ADCs and op-amps: aimed at motor control and digital power.
notes: Blank chips need an ICSP programmer/debugger (PICkit 4/5, MPLAB Snap or ICD); there is no factory bootloader.
Only the MP50x parts have CAN FD (1 controller); the cheaper dsPIC33CK...MP20x have none. Newer dsPIC33CK512MP60x adds a 2nd CAN FD and 64 KB RAM.
3.0-3.6 V supply only, but many pins are 5 V tolerant. Not a low-power part: sleep current is ~0.4 mA typical.
PWM outputs 8/16 (28-pin/48+ pin) high-resolution; ADC inputs 12/19/20/24 for 28/48/64/80 pins; 3 op-amps (2 on 28-pin).
The 3 SPI modules double as I2S (shared). 3 x 12-bit DACs feed the comparators; one has a pin output (DACOUT).

mcus.name: PIC32MZ EF
mcus.description: 200 MHz MIPS M-class MCU with double-precision FPU, 2 MB flash, 512 KB RAM, High-Speed USB with on-chip PHY, Ethernet MAC and two CAN 2.0B.
notes: Feature letter after 'EF': E/G = no CAN, F/H = 2x CAN 2.0B, K/M = CAN + crypto engine (AES/3DES/SHA). All have a hardware RNG. CAN is classic 2.0B only (no CAN FD).
252 MHz only with the '-250' speed-grade parts (-40 to 85 C); standard parts are 200 MHz.
64-pin parts: 4 SPI/I2S, 4 I2C, 24 ADC inputs and no EBI. ADC inputs 40/48 on 100/144-pin.
USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG with integrated PHY; Ethernet MAC (MII/RMII) needs an external PHY. SQI quad-SPI controller; no SD host controller.
Not a low-power part (sleep current ~1.5 mA typical). No ROM bootloader: needs an ICSP/JTAG programmer.
Arduino/PlatformIO support only via the legacy, unmaintained chipKIT core (e.g. chipKIT WiFire).

mcus.name: PIC32MK MCM
mcus.description: 120 MHz MIPS MCU with FPU and four CAN FD controllers, two USB, 7 fast ADCs, op-amps and motor-control PWM: a dense CAN FD motor/industrial chip.
notes: 4 CAN FD controllers (no classic-only CAN); the related PIC32MK MCF parts have 4 classic CAN 2.0B instead. External transceivers required.
2 full-speed USB OTG controllers, 4 op-amps, 5 comparators, 3 DACs, 6 QEI, 12 motor-control PWM generators (24 outputs).
Seven 12-bit SAR ADC cores; 42 analog inputs on 100-pin (26 on 64-pin).
Specs taken from Microchip's official PIC32MK-MC device pack (datasheet DS60001519); FPU listed there as single precision.
No ROM bootloader: needs an ICSP/JTAG programmer (PICkit 4/5, ICD). Not supported by Arduino/PlatformIO.

mcus.name: PIC32CX-BZ2
mcus.description: Low-cost Cortex-M4F wireless SoC with Bluetooth LE 5.2 and Zigbee 3.0/Thread, 1 MB flash and hardware crypto; also sold as certified WBZ451 modules.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: MPLAB Harmony v3 (PIC32CX-BZ2 / WBZ45x wireless SDK)

notes: SERCOMs (4 on 48-pin, 2 on 32-pin) are each USART/SPI, I2C on 3 of the 4 - totals are shared. No USB, no CAN, no touch controller.
29 GPIO on the 48-pin part only when the 32 kHz crystal is unused (27 otherwise); 16 on the 32-pin part.
TX power: up to +12 dBm (BZ25048) / ~+5 dBm (BZ24032). Needs RF matching/antenna design - the pre-certified WBZ451 (PCB antenna) / WBZ451H (+20 dBm) modules avoid this.
Deep sleep 1.7 uA with 8 KB backup RAM retained (1.46 uA without). Crypto: AES (incl. GCM), SHA, ECC/RSA (PUKCC), TRNG.
Matter is not listed in the data sheet; Thread is supported via Microchip's OpenThread stack.
No documented ROM bootloader: program over SWD.

mcus.name: nRF52810
mcus.description: Entry-level Bluetooth LE SoC (Cortex-M4, 192 KB flash) for simple beacons, tags and sensors where cost matters more than RAM or peripherals.
notes: No FPU and only 24 KB RAM: fine for a simple BLE peripheral, tight once the SoftDevice Controller and a real application are both in.
No USB, no NFC, no I2S. The QFN32 package only brings out 16 GPIOs.
Nordic has no ROM bootloader. Flash a blank chip over SWD (J-Link, CMSIS-DAP or a Pi Pico debugprobe).
Needs a 32 MHz crystal; the 32.768 kHz crystal is optional. Nordic's DC/DC needs an external inductor.
Bluetooth only (plus ANT and 2.4 GHz proprietary). The nRF52811 is the near pin-compatible step up with Thread/Zigbee and direction finding.
Ebyte E73-2G4M04S1A is a cheap pre-certified module, but it is often out of stock at LCSC.

mcus.name: nRF52832
mcus.description: The classic Bluetooth LE SoC: Cortex-M4F, 512 KB flash, NFC tag and a huge choice of cheap modules and community support.
notes: Serial instances are shared: SPI0/TWI0 and SPI1/TWI1 are the same hardware, SPI2 stands alone. So you get 3 SPI, or 2 I2C + 1 SPI, plus a single UART.
Only one UART and no USB. Plan on SWD for flashing and a USB-UART bridge if you need a console.
No ROM bootloader. Boards like the Adafruit Feather nRF52832 ship a serial DFU bootloader in flash, but a blank chip needs an SWD programmer.
NFC-A tag pins (P0.09/P0.10) are NFC by default. Set CONFIG_NFCT_PINS_AS_GPIOS / UICR to use them as GPIO.
Thread/Zigbee/Matter are not officially supported on the nRF52832. Use nRF52833/nRF52840 or newer for those.
The 256 KB / 32 KB QFAB variant is cheaper but tight for current nRF Connect SDK builds.

mcus.name: nRF52833
mcus.description: Mid-range nRF52 with USB, 512 KB flash, +8 dBm radio, Bluetooth Long Range/direction finding and Thread/Zigbee; the chip in the BBC micro:bit v2.
notes: Serial sharing: SPIM0/TWIM0 and SPIM1/TWIM1 share hardware; SPIM2, SPIM3 (32 MHz) and both UARTEs are separate. Max is 4 SPI, or 2 I2C + 2 SPI + 2 UART at once.
USB 2.0 Full-Speed is device-only (no host).
VDDH accepts 2.5-5.5 V (e.g. USB VBUS or Li-ion). In that mode the REG0 output that feeds VDD/GPIO defaults to 1.8 V; set UICR REGOUT0 to get 3.3 V I/O.
The QFN40 package brings out only 18 GPIOs. The aQFN73 has 42 but needs fine-pitch PCB rules (via-in-pad/0.5 mm inner rows).
No ROM bootloader; flash over SWD. The micro:bit v2 uses an interface MCU for drag-and-drop flashing.
Not an official Matter target in nRF Connect SDK (use nRF52840/nRF5340/nRF54L15). MicroPython runs on the micro:bit v2 through the separate micro:bit port, not upstream ports/nrf.
Arduino support comes through community cores (e.g. arduino-nRF5 for the micro:bit v2).

mcus.name: nRF52840
mcus.description: The go-to Bluetooth LE + Thread/Zigbee/Matter SoC with native USB, QSPI, 1 MB flash and 256 KB RAM; huge board ecosystem (Feather, XIAO, nice!nano).
notes: Serial sharing: SPIM0/TWIM0 and SPIM1/TWIM1 share hardware; SPIM2, SPIM3 (32 MHz) and both UARTEs are separate. Max is 4 SPI, or 2 I2C + 2 SPI + 2 UART at once.
USB 2.0 Full-Speed is device-only (no host).
No ROM bootloader. Most boards (Adafruit, Seeed XIAO, nice!nano) ship the Adafruit UF2 bootloader in flash, but a blank chip or bare module needs SWD.
VDDH accepts 2.5-5.5 V (USB VBUS or Li-ion directly). In that mode GPIO voltage comes from REG0, which defaults to 1.8 V; set UICR REGOUT0 for 3.3 V I/O.
The bare chip is aQFN73 only (0.5 mm pitch with inner rows, needs via-in-pad or fine-pitch PCB). Most hobby designs use a pre-certified module such as Raytac MDBT50Q or Ebyte E73-2G4M08S1C.
The QSPI XIP window is 128 MB; 16 MB is a conservative practical figure. Mainline MicroPython, CircuitPython and Arduino (Adafruit nRF52 core / Arduino mbed) all support it.

mcus.name: nRF5340
mcus.description: Dual Cortex-M33 (128 MHz app + 64 MHz network core) for LE Audio, Matter and Thread, with USB, QSPI, 1 MB + 256 KB flash and TrustZone security.
notes: Memory figures are for the application core. The network core adds its own 256 KB flash and 64 KB RAM and normally runs the radio stack, with the nRF Connect SDK handling the IPC.

The app core has 4 serial boxes, each usable as UARTE, SPIM or TWIM, plus a dedicated 32 MHz SPIM4. So max is 4 UART, 4 I2C or 5 SPI (counts shared). The network core has one more serial box of its own.
USB 2.0 Full-Speed is device-only. QSPI runs at up to 96 MHz with XIP and on-the-fly decryption.
Running at 64 MHz is more efficient (73 CoreMark/mA vs 66 at 128 MHz). Sleep figure is System ON with the network core RTC running.
No ROM bootloader; flash both cores over SWD. Only aQFN94/WLCSP packages, so most hobby PCBs use a module (Raytac MDBT53, u-blox NORA-B1, Ezurio BL5340).
No Arduino, MicroPython or CircuitPython port: this is a nRF Connect SDK / Zephyr (or Rust embassy) part.

mcus.name: nRF54L15
mcus.description: Nordic's newest mainstream BLE/Thread/Matter SoC: 128 MHz Cortex-M33 plus RISC-V coprocessor, 1.5 MB RRAM, Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding, in an easy QFN48. Cheaper than the nRF52840.
notes: No USB and no QSPI peripheral. QSPI is available only as a 'SoftPeripheral' running on the RISC-V (VPR) coprocessor.
Five serial interfaces: one high-speed instance (UARTE00/SPIM00 up to 32 MHz, no TWI) plus four shared ones, each UARTE, SPIM or TWIM. So max is 5 UART, 5 SPI or 4 I2C (counts shared).
SAADC is 12-bit at 250 ksps, 14-bit at 31.25 ksps or 10-bit at 2 Msps.
Sleep figure is System ON idle with GRTC and all 256 KB RAM retained; 0.8 µA in System OFF with GRTC wake-up. About 20 µA/MHz running CoreMark from RRAM.
Uses RRAM instead of flash and is supported only by nRF Connect SDK v2.6+ / Zephyr (no legacy nRF5 SDK). Some peripherals are tied to specific GPIO ports (power domains), so check pin assignments.
Other packages: QFN40 (24 GPIO), QFN52 (35 GPIO), CSP47 (32 GPIO). Raytac AN54LQ/AN54LV modules exist; Seeed XIAO nRF54L15 is a cheap board.

mcus.name: nRF9151
mcus.description: Pre-certified LTE-M/NB-IoT + GNSS (and DECT NR+) system-in-package with a user-programmable Cortex-M33, for battery-powered cellular IoT trackers and sensors.
notes: SiP with integrated LTE-M/NB-IoT modem (3GPP Rel. 14, bands 1-5, 8, 12, 13, 17-20, 25, 26, 28, 65, 66, 85), GNSS receiver, RF front end and PMIC. Needs a SIM (nano-SIM/eSIM/iSIM), an LTE antenna and a GNSS antenna.
Power Class 3 (23 dBm) and Class 5 (20 dBm). DECT NR+ needs separate modem firmware; NTN (satellite) bands are being added.
No Bluetooth/Thread radio. Pair it with an nRF52/nRF54L if you need BLE.
4 serial boxes, each UARTE, SPIM or TWIM, so max is 4 of any one type (counts are shared). VBAT 3.0-5.5 V; I/O voltage comes from VDD_GPIO (1.8-3.3 V). TX current peaks need a stiff supply.
No ROM bootloader; flash over SWD. The modem firmware is a separate Nordic binary, and the app uses the nRF Modem library (nRF Connect SDK).

PSM floor current is not listed here because the official figure couldn't be confirmed. LCSC stock is often zero; DigiKey/Mouser or the Nordic Thingy:91 X / nRF9151 DK are alternatives for prototyping.

mcus.name: LPC55S69
mcus.description: Dual 150 MHz Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, crypto/PUF, high-speed USB with on-chip PHY plus full-speed USB and an SD/SDIO host; a secure, well-documented general-purpose MCU.
notes: Flexcomm 0-7 are each ONE of USART / SPI / I2C / I2S at a time, Flexcomm 8 is a dedicated high-speed SPI: the per-type counts are not simultaneous (max 9 serial blocks in total).
USB1 is high-speed host/device with on-chip HS PHY; USB0 is full-speed host/device with crystal-less device mode. Both can run at the same time.
The second Cortex-M33 (CPU1) has no FPU, DSP extension, MPU or TrustZone.
ROM ISP over USB0/USB1 (HID class, use blhost / MCUXpresso Secure Provisioning), UART (Flexcomm 0), SPI and I2C - no programmer needed.
No QSPI/XIP interface; the top of the 640 KB flash holds the protected flash region (PFR), so slightly less is available to applications.
HLQFP100 and HTQFP64 have a 3.4 x 3.4 mm exposed ground pad; KiCad's plain LQFP footprints lack it.
Crypto: AES-256, SHA-2, CASPER (ECC/RSA), PUF key storage, PRINCE on-the-fly flash encryption, TRNG, secure boot. PowerQuad DSP accelerator.
Rust: lpc55-hal (used by SoloKeys Solo 2 / Nitrokey 3 firmware).

mcus.name: LPC845
mcus.description: Low-cost 30 MHz Cortex-M0+ with a switch matrix that routes any function to any pin, 5 USARTs, 4 I2C, two DACs and capacitive touch, in hand-solderable LQFP.
notes: Switch matrix: USART/SPI/I2C/SCT functions can be assigned to almost any pin.
ROM ISP over USART0 (also I2C/SPI); no USB, so use a USB-UART adapter or SWD.
HVQFN33 (JHI33) version has no capacitive touch, only one DAC and 29 GPIO.
No RTC - only a self-wake-up timer (WKT). One I2C is Fast-mode Plus on true open-drain pins.
LPC845-BRK breakout board has an on-board CMSIS-DAP debug probe and is very cheap.
LPC844 is the cut-down sibling (2 USART, 2 I2C, 8 KB SRAM, no DAC/touch).

mcus.name: LPC1768
mcus.description: Classic 100 MHz Cortex-M3 (the original mbed) with Ethernet MAC, USB host/device/OTG, two classic CAN channels and 512 KB flash in an LQFP-100.
notes: Both CAN channels are classic CAN 2.0B only - no CAN-FD.
Ethernet MAC needs an external RMII PHY; USB is full-speed device/host/OTG with on-chip PHY.
SPI count = 1 legacy SPI + 2 SSP controllers.
ROM ISP over UART0 (Flash Magic / lpc21isp); no USB bootloader in ROM (the mbed board uses a separate interface chip).
I/O pins are 5 V tolerant. LPC1769 is the pin-compatible 120 MHz version.
Mature 2009-era part: expensive per MHz compared to modern Cortex-M4/M33 MCUs; mainly for legacy mbed designs. Also offered in TFBGA100.

mcus.name: MCXA153
mcus.description: Cheap 96 MHz Cortex-M33 with crystal-less full-speed USB device, 16-bit ADC and motor-control PWM; NXP's modern entry-level MCU with USB/UART ROM bootloader.
notes: This Cortex-M33 has NO FPU, DSP extension, TrustZone or MPU.
USB is full-speed DEVICE only (crystal-less), no host.
ROM ISP over LPUART and USB (SPI/I2C ISP not available on A14x/A15x) - no programmer needed.
No RTC peripheral (wake timer / OS event timer only).
Also has 1x I3C (can talk to legacy I2C devices), eQDC quadrature decoder and FlexPWM with 6 outputs; ADC inputs depend on package (fewer on QFN-32).
MCXA152 = 64 KB flash / 16 KB RAM; MCXA14x = 48 MHz versions. FRDM-MCXA153 is the low-cost dev board.

mcus.name: MCXN947
mcus.description: Dual 150 MHz Cortex-M33 with NPU, 2 MB flash, 2x CAN-FD, high-speed USB with PHY, Ethernet, SDHC and rich analog; a feature-packed modern NXP MCU.
notes: 10 LP_FLEXCOMM blocks, each configurable as LPUART, LPSPI or LPI2C (or LPUART+LPI2C together): uart/i2c/spi counts are per type, not simultaneous (10 blocks total). Plus 2x I3C.
Both FlexCAN controllers support CAN-FD.
100-pin HLQFP (VKLT) has NO high-speed USB, uSDHC, capacitive touch or smart-card interface and only 78 GPIO; use VFBGA-184 or HDQFP-172 for the full feature set.
USB: one high-speed host/device with on-chip HS PHY + one full-speed host/device with on-chip PHY. Ethernet is 10/100 MAC (RMII/MII, external PHY).
Secondary Cortex-M33 core lacks the FPU/TrustZone/MPU of the primary core. eIQ Neutron NPU, PowerQuad DSP, EdgeLock secure enclave.
No dedicated LCD or camera controller: FlexIO / SmartDMA drive 8080 displays and parallel cameras in the SDK.
FlexSPI (octal/quad NOR, HyperRAM/PSRAM, XIP); external flash/PSRAM limits here are approximate.
HDQFP-172 uses two staggered rows of 0.65 mm-pitch leads. ROM ISP includes USB and UART.

mcus.name: i.MX RT1011
mcus.description: The cheapest 500 MHz Cortex-M7 in a hand-solderable LQFP-80, with high-speed USB OTG (on-chip PHY) and QSPI XIP; great for fast audio/USB gadgets.
notes: Flashless: needs an external QSPI NOR flash on FlexSPI (XIP). 128 KB FlexRAM is shared between ITCM/DTCM/OCRAM.
ROM serial downloader over USB (HID) and LPUART1 - flash with NXP MCUXpresso Secure Provisioning / blhost / MCUBootUtility, no programmer needed.
USB 2.0 OTG with integrated high-speed PHY; 24 MHz crystal required.
Single 3.3 V supply into the on-chip DCDC (needs external inductor); I/O banks can be 1.8 V or 3.3 V.
No CAN, Ethernet or SD host. 2x SAI + SPDIF + MQS for audio; DCP (AES-128/SHA-256) and HAB secure boot.
MIMXRT1011DAE5A is consumer grade (0-95 C Tj, 500 MHz); MIMXRT1011CAE4A is industrial (400 MHz).
External-flash limit is the approximate FlexSPI memory-mapped window.

mcus.name: i.MX RT1062
mcus.description: 600 MHz Cortex-M7 with 1 MB SRAM, 2x high-speed USB, 2x Ethernet, 2x SD, LCD and camera interfaces; the Teensy 4.x chip with a huge Arduino ecosystem.
notes: 3 FlexCAN controllers but only CAN3 supports CAN-FD; CAN1/CAN2 are classic CAN 2.0B.
Flashless: boots/XIPs from external QSPI NOR on FlexSPI; FlexSPI2 can host QSPI PSRAM (Teensy 4.1 takes 2x 8 MB); SEMC adds SDRAM/parallel NOR/NAND.
1 MB SRAM = 512 KB FlexRAM (configurable ITCM/DTCM/OCRAM) + 512 KB OCRAM.
2x USB 2.0 OTG with integrated high-speed PHYs; 2x 10/100 Ethernet MACs (RMII, external PHY); 2x uSDHC (SD 3.0/eMMC 4.5).
BGA only: DVL/CVL = 10x10 mm 0.65 mm pitch, DVJ/CVJ = 12x12 mm 0.8 mm pitch - plan a 4+ layer PCB.
D-grade (consumer) runs 600 MHz; C-grade (industrial, e.g. CVL5B) is limited to 528 MHz. B-revision silicon replaces A.
ROM serial downloader over USB HID and UART. LCD (eLCDIF), parallel camera (CSI) and PXP 2D engine are included on RT1062 (not on RT1061).

mcus.name: i.MX RT1176
mcus.description: 1 GHz Cortex-M7 plus 400 MHz Cortex-M4 with 2 MB SRAM, 3x CAN-FD, 2x HS USB, gigabit Ethernet, MIPI-DSI/CSI and 2D GPU; an MPU-class MCU for HMI and gateways.
notes: All 3 FlexCAN controllers support CAN-FD.
3 Ethernet MACs: 10/100 (IEEE1588), 1 GbE with AVB and 1 GbE with TSN; gigabit needs an RGMII PHY.
2x USB 2.0 OTG with integrated high-speed PHYs; 2x uSDHC (SD 3.0 / eMMC 5.0).
Flashless: boots from FlexSPI NOR (two FlexSPI ports, HyperRAM/PSRAM capable); SEMC supports 8/16/32-bit SDRAM.
Display: eLCDIF + LCDIFv2 + MIPI-DSI (2-lane, PHY integrated), 2D vector GPU and PXP; camera: parallel CSI + MIPI-CSI2.
2 MB SRAM total incl. 512 KB M7 TCM and 256 KB M4 TCM. Crypto: CAAM, PUF, OTFAD/IEE, HAB secure boot.
289 MAPBGA (14x14 mm, 0.8 mm) only - realistically a 6-layer PCB. Consumer DVMAA runs the M7 at 1 GHz, industrial CVM8A at 800 MHz.
ADC channel count is conservative (2x 12-bit ADC); external-flash/PSRAM limits are approximate.

mcus.name: S32K144
mcus.description: AEC-Q100 automotive Cortex-M4F running from 2.7-5.5 V with 3 FlexCAN (1 CAN-FD), 512 KB flash and LIN-capable UARTs; cheap and robust for 5 V/12 V vehicle electronics.
notes: 3 FlexCAN controllers but only ONE (CAN0) supports CAN-FD; S32K146 has 2 FD, S32K148 has 3 FD.
Single 2.7-5.5 V supply: runs directly from 5 V with 5 V I/O.
Speed grade: 'H' parts run 80 MHz, 'U' parts 112 MHz in HSRUN (no flash/EEPROM writes or CSEc in HSRUN).
Feature letter: 'F' = CAN-FD + FlexIO, 'A' = CAN-FD + FlexIO + CSEc security (AES-128 secure boot/keys). HFT parts have no CSEc.
No ROM serial bootloader: a blank chip must be programmed over SWD/JTAG (NXP provides CAN/UART bootloader reference code).
FlexRAM can emulate up to 4 KB EEPROM backed by 64 KB D-Flash. LPUARTs support LIN; FlexIO can emulate extra UART/SPI/I2C/I2S.
ADC: 2x 12-bit SAR, 16 channels each on the 100-pin package.

mcus.name: S32K344
mcus.description: ASIL-D lockstep 160 MHz Cortex-M7 with 6 CAN-FD controllers, 16 LPUARTs, 4 MB flash and 100 Mbit Ethernet, running from 3.3 or 5 V; a top pick for multi-CAN-FD automotive tools.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: S32 Design Studio + S32K3 RTD (AUTOSAR MCAL)

notes: All 6 FlexCAN controllers support CAN-FD.
Cortex-M7 in lockstep (ASIL D) with single-precision FPU; 512 KB SRAM incl. 192 KB TCM, plus 128 KB data flash. HSE_B security engine (AES, secure boot).
Feature letter: 'E' parts (S32K344EH...) have a 10/100 Ethernet MAC + 2 SAI; 'N' parts have neither.
Single 2.97-5.5 V supply (3.3 V or 5 V systems). No USB.
Packages: 172-pin HDQFP (16x16 mm, two staggered rows of 0.65 mm-pitch leads) or 257 MAPBGA (14x14 mm, 0.8 mm); the data sheet also lists a 100-pin LQFP.
No serial ROM bootloader: program over SWD/JTAG; handle the HSE firmware/lifecycle carefully.
ADC (3x 12-bit SAR, up to 24 inputs each), GPIO and eMIOS PWM counts are approximate/conservative - check the IO muxing sheet for the exact package.
16 LPUARTs all LIN-capable; FlexIO (32 ch) can emulate extra UART/SPI/I2C/I2S/SENT.

mcus.name: MKL25Z128
mcus.description: 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with USB OTG full-speed, 16-bit ADC, DAC and 16 capacitive-touch channels; the chip on the classic FRDM-KL25Z board.
notes: No ROM bootloader: a blank chip must be programmed over SWD (FRDM-KL25Z uses its OpenSDA probe). KL27/KL17 add a ROM bootloader.
USB 2.0 full-speed OTG with on-chip transceiver and a 5 V-to-3.3 V regulator (VREGIN) that can power the chip from USB VBUS.
UART0 is a low-power UART (LPSCI) plus two standard UARTs; SPIs are 8-bit.
Also sold as 32/64 KB-flash MKL25Z32/MKL25Z64 variants.
Legacy Freescale-era part: LCSC stock is thin and qty-1 prices high; NXP's MCX A series is the modern replacement.

mcus.name: STC8H8K64U
mcus.description: Cheap 1T 8051 with native USB and a USB-HID bootloader (flash with just a cable), 64 KB flash, 4 UARTs, 12-bit ADC and a 1.9-5.5 V supply.
notes: USB is full-speed device only. Factory ISP runs over USB-HID (hold P3.2 low at power-up) or UART with the STC-ISP tool; no programmer needed. Newer (B/C/D) silicon also supports USB debugging.
RAM is 8 KB xdata + 256 B idata (+1.25 KB USB buffer). 8-channel advanced PWM (PWMA/PWMB, with dead time); no hardware DAC.
LCM interface drives 8080/6800 TFT panels (not on 'A' silicon). Has RTC, DMA, 16-bit MDU and a comparator.
Internal oscillator up to 45 MHz, no crystal needed even for USB. Documentation is primarily Chinese; English datasheet available.

mcus.name: M031
mcus.description: Long-lived Nuvoton Cortex-M0 family (48 MHz, 16-128 KB flash) with 1.8-3.6 V supply, 5 V tolerant I/O and a 2 MSPS 12-bit ADC.
notes: Huge family (16 KB-512 KB); figures here cover the listed parts. 256/512 KB M031xG/xI parts run at 72 MHz and add RTC, QSPI and more UARTs. M032 adds crystal-less USB FS device.
Nuvoton calls the 4x4 mm QFN 'QFN33' (exposed pad = pin 33, VSS). The x8+ parts add a USCI (configurable UART/SPI/I2C) and 2 comparators; no RTC on these densities.
ISP needs a loader in LDROM (Nuvoton supplies UART/USB ISP code); plan on a Nu-Link (SWD) for the first program since blank-chip ROM ISP is not documented.
TSSOP-20 part had very low LCSC stock when checked.

mcus.name: M487
mcus.description: 192 MHz Cortex-M4F with USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG (on-chip PHY) plus FS OTG, Ethernet MAC, 2x CAN, 2x SD host and crypto engines.
notes: USB 2.0 HS OTG with on-chip PHY on all parts; the extra USB FS OTG controller is only on LQFP-128/144 (M487SIDAE has HS only).
Ethernet is a 10/100 MAC with RMII (external PHY required). Crypto: AES, DES/3DES, SHA/HMAC, ECC, RNG.
SPIM maps external quad-SPI flash with a 32 KB cache; the maximum size is not stated in the datasheet (16 MB assumed). EBI provides an 8/16-bit LCD parallel bus.
Datasheet mentions a 32 KB ROM boot loader with native ISP, but interfaces are not documented there; keep a Nu-Link/SWD probe handy. LCSC stock is low and prices are high (~$6.5+).
Nuvoton maintains a MicroPython fork (OpenNuvoton) for NuMaker-IoT-M487; not upstream.

mcus.name: K210
mcus.description: Dual-core 64-bit RISC-V AI SoC (400 MHz, 8 MB SRAM) with a CNN accelerator (KPU), audio processor and camera port; the chip in Sipeed Maix boards.
notes: No internal flash, no ADC, no USB and no radio: boards add SPI flash, a USB-UART bridge (flashed with kflash over the ROM UART ISP) and often an ESP32/ESP8285 for WiFi.
8 MB on-chip SRAM = 6 MB general + 2 MB reserved for the KPU when AI is used. 400 MHz nominal (commonly overclocked to 600 MHz+).
Needs 0.9 V core plus 1.8 V/3.3 V I/O rails; I/O banks are 1.8 or 3.3 V. Fine-pitch 0.65 mm BGA-144, so most people use a module (Sipeed M1/M1W).
48 pins are freely mappable via the FPIOA. SPI: 2 masters (quad/octal capable) + 1 slave-only SPI; SPI3 is dedicated to boot flash. Extras: FFT accelerator, AES/SHA256, 3x I2S with mic-array APU.
MicroPython means Sipeed's MaixPy port; Arduino means Maixduino. Successor is the Kendryte K230.

mcus.name: PY32F002A
mcus.description: One of the cheapest 32-bit MCUs (~$0.10 in volume): 24 MHz Cortex-M0+, 20 KB flash, runs from 1.7-5.5 V, SOP-8 to TSSOP-20, UART-flashable.
notes: Bare-bones: 1 USART, 1 I2C (100/400 kHz, 7-bit only), 1 SPI, TIM1 + TIM16 + LPTIM, 2 comparators, no DMA, no RTC.
ADC external channels depend on package (4 on SOP-8, up to 9 on QFN-20).
Flash over UART with the ROM bootloader (BOOT0 high at reset, any USB-serial adapter) or over standard Arm SWD; OpenOCD/pyOCD need the Puya device pack.
Datasheets and reference manuals are mostly Chinese; community GCC template: github.com/IOsetting/py32f0-template.

mcus.name: PY32F003
mcus.description: Ultra-cheap 32 MHz Cortex-M0+ with up to 64 KB flash / 8 KB RAM, 2 USARTs, DMA and RTC, running from 1.7-5.5 V for about $0.15 in volume.
notes: The digit after the pinout code sets memory: F18 = 64 KB/8 KB, F16 = 32 KB/4 KB, F14 = 16 KB/2 KB. SOP-8/DFN-8/SOP-16/MSOP-10 versions also exist (SOP-8 has 1 USART).
Timers: TIM1 + TIM3 + TIM14/16/17 + LPTIM; 3-channel DMA; 2 comparators. No USB.
Flash over UART with the ROM bootloader (BOOT0 high at reset, any USB-serial adapter) or over standard Arm SWD; OpenOCD/pyOCD need the Puya device pack.
Datasheets and reference manuals are mostly Chinese; community GCC template: github.com/IOsetting/py32f0-template.

mcus.name: PY32F030
mcus.description: Low-cost 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 64 KB flash, 2 SPI, 2 USART, up to 30 GPIO and a 1.7-5.5 V supply; a cheap 5 V-capable STM32F030-class part.
notes: K1x/K2x and F1x/F2x are two different pinouts of the same die (K2 = 30 GPIO, K1 = 28 GPIO); check the pinout table before copying an STM32F030 layout.
Extras: 4-digit 7-segment LED scan driver, 4 high-sink (up to 80 mA) GPIOs, LSE crystal + RTC, 3-channel DMA, 2 comparators. No USB.
Flash over UART with the ROM bootloader (BOOT0 high at reset, any USB-serial adapter) or over standard Arm SWD; OpenOCD/pyOCD need the Puya device pack.
Datasheets and reference manuals are mostly Chinese; community GCC template: github.com/IOsetting/py32f0-template.

mcus.name: RP2040
mcus.description: Dual-core Cortex-M0+ with 8 PIO state machines; cheap, hugely popular, drag-and-drop UF2 flashing over USB.
notes: Needs an external QSPI flash chip (e.g. W25Q16) and a 12 MHz crystal.
SD card, I2S, extra UARTs, WS2812 and even CAN can be done in PIO.
Certified for 200 MHz operation since 2024 (SDK 2.1+).

mcus.name: RP2350
mcus.description: RP2040 successor with dual Cortex-M33 (or Hazard3 RISC-V) cores at 150 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, 12 PIO state machines and secure boot; still cheap and UF2-flashable.
mcus.core: Arm Cortex-M33 (or Hazard3 RISC-V, selectable at boot)
notes: RP2350A/RP2354A (QFN-60) have 30 GPIO and 4 ADC inputs; RP2350B/RP2354B (QFN-80) have 48 GPIO and 8 ADC inputs.
RP2350A/B need an external QSPI flash and a 12 MHz crystal; RP2354A/B have 2 MB flash stacked in the package (same pinout).
3 PIO blocks (12 state machines) plus an HSTX block (e.g. DVI output); I2S, SD card and extra UARTs are done in PIO.
A second QSPI chip-select (on a GPIO) can add up to 16 MB of PSRAM or more flash.
Arm cores have a single-precision FPU and a double-precision coprocessor; the Hazard3 RISC-V cores have no FPU.
No calendar RTC (removed vs RP2040); the always-on timer keeps time in low-power states.
On-chip switching regulator takes 2.7-5.5 V on VREG_VIN, but IOVDD/VREG_AVDD still need 3.3 V.
Early A2 silicon has erratum RP2350-E9 (GPIO leakage, pull-downs unreliable); fixed from stepping A3, current stock is A4.
Deep-sleep figure is the P1.7 power-down state from the datasheet, including the external flash supply.

mcus.name: RA0E1
mcus.description: Very cheap (~$0.50) 32 MHz Cortex-M23 that runs straight from 1.6-5.5 V with ~0.2 uA standby; good for small 5 V sensor, glue-logic and battery jobs in 16- to 32-pin packages.
notes: No ROM bootloader and no MD/boot-mode pin: a blank chip can only be flashed over SWD (J-Link, E2 Lite, or the J-Link on the FPB-RA0E1 board). Field updates over UART need your own bootloader.

Serial ports come from a 6-channel Serial Array Unit (SAU): up to 3 UARTs (one LIN-capable), 3 simplified SPI or 3 simplified (master-only) I2C, one function per channel. There is also one UARTA and one IICA. uart = 3 SAU UARTs + UARTA; spi = the 3 SAU simplified-SPI channels (there is no dedicated SPI block), so UART and SPI counts compete for the same SAU channels.
Runs directly from 1.6-5.5 V, so a 5 V supply is fine; HOCO runs at 24/32 MHz with no crystal needed.
No USB, CAN, DAC, capacitive touch or crypto engine (TRNG only). The 12-bit ADC has 10 inputs on 32-pin parts and 6 on the 20-pin package.
Timer Array Unit: 8 x 16-bit channels (up to 7 PWM outputs) plus a 32-bit interval timer.
32 KB flash versions (R7FA0E1053...) also exist. The TSSOP-20 (CSD) comes in 64 KB only; an LSSOP-20 (CSC) is also offered.
The QFN-32 exposed pad is 3.2 x 3.2 mm. KiCad has 3.1 and 3.3 mm variants but no exact match.

mcus.name: RA2E1
mcus.description: Low-power 48 MHz Cortex-M23 that runs from 1.6-5.5 V, with up to 30 capacitive-touch channels and AES; a cheap 5 V-capable general-purpose MCU in packages from 25 to 64 pins.
notes: 4 SCI channels (SCI0/1/2/9; 3 on packages of 36 pins or fewer). Each one works as a UART, simple SPI or simple I2C (master-only), so UART, SPI and I2C share them. On top of that there is 1 dedicated IIC and 1 dedicated SPI.
ROM SCI boot mode: hold MD (P201) low at reset and flash over a UART with Renesas Flash Programmer. There is no USB.
Runs directly from 1.6-5.5 V and needs no crystal (HOCO up to 64 MHz, trimmed). No USB, CAN, DAC or SD host.
CTSU2 capacitive touch: 30 channels on 64-pin, 20 on 48-pin and 11 on 32-pin parts. The 12-bit ADC has 13 inputs (10 on 32-pin).
Timers: 1 x 32-bit + 6 x 16-bit GPT (14 PWM outputs on 48/64-pin) and 2 low-power AGT. AES-128/256 and TRNG on chip.
Not supported by upstream Zephyr (only RA2A1/RA2L1 are). Use Renesas FSP / e2 studio.
A 14 x 14 mm 0.8 mm-pitch LQFP-64 (CFK) is also available.

mcus.name: RA4M1
mcus.description: The Arduino Uno R4 chip: a 48 MHz Cortex-M4F that runs from 1.6-5.5 V with USB FS (host/device), one classic CAN, segment LCD, 14-bit ADC, DAC and capacitive touch.
notes: R7FA4M1AB3CFM (LQFP-64) is the MCU on the Arduino Uno R4 Minima and WiFi.
Runs directly from 5 V, and USB still works then: feed 3.8-5.5 V to VCC_USB_LDO and the on-chip regulator makes the 3.3 V USB supply.
CAN is one classic CAN 2.0B controller (no CAN-FD) and needs an external transceiver.
4 SCI channels (SCI0/1/2/9). Each works as a UART, simple SPI or simple I2C, so they are shared. There are also 2 dedicated IIC and 2 dedicated SPI (1 SPI on the 40-pin QFN).

ROM boot mode, selected with the MD pin, supports both SCI (UART) and USB through Renesas Flash Programmer (a Renesas protocol, not DFU). Arduino boards add their own USB bootloader (double-tap reset).
SSIE (I2S) is only on 100-pin packages. The segment LCD controller is on 64/100-pin parts. The 14-bit ADC has 25 inputs on 100-pin, 18 on 64-pin and 14 on 48-pin.
One 12-bit DAC output. The two 8-bit DACs only feed the low-power comparators. There are also 4 op-amps.
No SDHI/SDIO and no QSPI: use SPI mode for microSD.
The QFN-48 exists in two drawings (PWQN0048KB-A with a 5.5 mm EP, PWQN0048KC-A with 5.3 mm). A 5.3 mm land suits both.
activeUaPerMhz uses CoreMark from flash (16.4 mA at 48 MHz). A while(1) loop draws about half that.

mcus.name: RA4E2
mcus.description: 100 MHz Cortex-M33 with one CAN-FD channel, USB FS device, I3C and I2S in small 32- to 64-pin packages; one of the cheapest ways to get CAN-FD on a modern Arm core.
notes: One CANFD channel (classic CAN and CAN-FD, ISO 11898-1). It needs an external transceiver.
USBFS is device-only (no host) and is missing on the 32-pin QFN. ROM boot mode supports SCI (UART), USB and SWD.

Only 2 SCI channels (SCI0, SCI9), each a UART, simple SPI or simple I2C. There is no classic IIC block: I2C is done by the single I3C module, which also talks to legacy I2C devices and is counted as i2c here. There are also 2 dedicated SPI.
Supply is 2.7-3.6 V only (no 5 V operation), though some pins are 5 V tolerant.
No capacitive touch, QSPI or crypto accelerator (TrustZone + TRNG only). There is 1 DAC channel and the 12-bit ADC has 12 inputs on 64-pin parts.

Deep Software Standby draws about 4.2 uA typ (about 16 uA when keeping 1 KB standby SRAM). Plain Software Standby is about 1.4 mA on this process. Active current is about 8.2 mA running CoreMark at 100 MHz.
The QFN-32 exposed pad is 3.2 x 3.2 mm, and KiCad has no exact match.

mcus.name: RA6M5
mcus.description: 200 MHz Cortex-M33 with 2 MB flash, 512 KB RAM, Ethernet, USB HS (internal PHY) + USB FS, two CAN-FD, SDHI, QSPI/OSPI and a strong crypto engine; a connected-gateway workhorse.
notes: CAN: 2 channels. Part numbers starting R7FA6M5B... (feature set B, listed here) support CAN-FD on both channels. R7FA6M5A... parts are classic CAN only, so order the B parts if you need CAN-FD. External transceivers are required.
USBHS (480 Mbit/s, on-chip HS PHY, host/device) is only bonded out on the 176-pin LQFP/BGA and 100-pin BGA. The 144-pin and 100-pin LQFP parts have USBFS only.
Ethernet: one 10/100 MAC with an external PHY. The 176-pin and 100-pin LQFP are RMII-only, the 144-pin supports MII and RMII, and the 100-pin BGA has no Ethernet.
One SDHI/MMC host (4-bit SD, up to 8-bit eMMC).
10 SCI channels (9 on the 100-pin BGA), each a UART, simple SPI or simple I2C, so they are shared. There are also 3 dedicated IIC and 2 SPI.
QSPI (64 MB memory-mapped window) and OSPI (128 MB CS0 + 256 MB CS1 windows, OctaFlash/OctaRAM) are both present.
Supply is 2.7-3.6 V only. ROM boot mode supports SCI (UART) and USB (Renesas Flash Programmer).
Used on the Arduino Portenta C33 (Arduino core, PlatformIO, MicroPython).
ADC: 2 x 12-bit units with up to 26 distinct inputs on 176-pin (22 on 144-pin, 17 on 100-pin). CTSU touch: 15 / 20 / 12 channels on 176 / 144 / 100-pin LQFP.
Deep Software Standby draws about 4.8 uA typ. Ordinary Software Standby is about 2.1 mA typ on this process. Active current is about 22 mA running CoreMark at 200 MHz.
A 1 MB (R7FA6M5BF...) version and BGA versions are also available.

mcus.name: RA8M1
mcus.description: Cortex-M85 with Helium at up to 480 MHz, 2 MB flash, 1 MB SRAM, Ethernet, USB HS + FS, two CAN-FD, two SDHI, OSPI and a camera input; Renesas' high-end MCU for DSP/ML and gateways.
notes: The maximum CPU clock depends on the package: 480 MHz only on the 224-pin BGA (Tj up to 105 C). It is 400 MHz on the 176/144-pin LQFP and 169-pin BGA, and 360 MHz on the 100-pin LQFP (240 MHz above Tj 105 C).
Two CANFD channels (classic CAN and CAN-FD) on every package. External transceivers are required.
USBHS (480 Mbit/s, on-chip HS PHY, host/device) is only on the 224/169-pin BGA and 176-pin LQFP. The 144-pin and 100-pin LQFP have USBFS only. USB needs VCC of at least 3.0 V.

Two SDHI/MMC hosts and one 10/100 Ethernet MAC (MII/RMII, external PHY). OSPI (xSPI/HyperBus, 2 x 256 MB windows) is on all packages. The SDRAM controller (128 MB window) is only on the 224/176/169-pin packages.
6 SCI channels (UART, simple SPI or simple I2C, shared) plus 2 dedicated IIC, 1 I3C (counted as i2c) and 2 SPI. SSIE (I2S): 2, or 1 on 100-pin.
CEU camera interface: 16-bit on 224/176/169-pin, 8-bit on 144-pin, none on 100-pin. No capacitive touch and no LCD controller (see RA8D1 for graphics).
1 MB SRAM = 896 KB user SRAM + 128 KB TCM. ADC: 2 x 12-bit units with up to 21 distinct inputs on 224-pin BGA and 20 on 176-pin LQFP.
Runs from 1.68-3.6 V and has an optional on-chip DC-DC regulator. Deep Software Standby (mode 3) draws about 1.6 uA typ in DCDC mode.
ROM boot modes: SCI (UART), USB and JTAG (Renesas Flash Programmer).

mcus.name: EFR32MG24
mcus.description: Matter/Thread/Zigbee + Bluetooth LE SoC with a 78 MHz Cortex-M33, 1.5 MB flash, 256 KB RAM, AI/ML accelerator and Secure Vault; used in XIAO MG24 and Arduino Nano Matter.
notes: Serial: 1 USART (UART/SPI/I2S/IrDA/SmartCard) + 2 EUSART (UART/SPI) + 2 I2C. The UART and SPI counts share those 3 blocks.

IADC is 12-bit @ 1 Msps or 16-bit @ 76.9 ksps. Select OPNs (B310/B110/B120, 'ADC' pinout with 28 GPIO) add high-speed and high-accuracy (16-bit ENOB) modes. Any GPIO on ports A-D can be an analog input via ABUS.
2 VDACs (2 channels each), 2 analog comparators, keypad scanner, and an MVP matrix-vector accelerator for TensorFlow Lite Micro.
TX power: B2x0/x20 parts reach +19.5 dBm; x10 parts +10 dBm. Bluetooth Channel Sounding needs a 40 MHz crystal and is limited to 10 dBm.
No USB and no ROM UART bootloader. Flash a blank chip over SWD (J-Link / Simplicity Link debugger); the Gecko Bootloader (UART/OTA) is optional and lives in flash.
Arduino core (Silicon Labs) supports XIAO MG24, SparkFun Thing Plus Matter (MGM240P), Nano Matter and the xG24 kits. CircuitPython supports the xG24 kits and Thing Plus Matter.
MGM240P module: pre-certified, crystal and antenna on board, 36 pads at 1.0 mm pitch. The PB32 version is +20 dBm.

mcus.name: EFR32BG22
mcus.description: Low-cost, ultra-low-power Bluetooth LE SoC (76.8 MHz Cortex-M33, 512 KB flash) with direction finding (AoA/AoD), ideal for coin-cell sensors, tags and beacons.
notes: Bluetooth LE only (no 802.15.4), so no Thread/Zigbee/Matter. The EFR32MG22/MG24 are the 802.15.4 siblings.
Serial: 2 USART (UART/SPI/I2S) + 1 low-energy EUART (UART only, works in EM2) + 2 I2C. PDM microphone input; no DAC. Max TX power is about +6 dBm.
Sleep figure is EM2 with RAM retention and RTC. Active current is about 27 µA/MHz.
