No USB and no ROM UART bootloader. Flash over SWD; the Gecko Bootloader (UART/OTA) is optional and lives in flash.
BGM220P is the pre-certified module (BGM220 Explorer Kit, supported by the Silicon Labs Arduino core). The module pad pitch here is approximate; use Silicon Labs' land pattern.
Exposed-pad sizes aren't listed because the Silicon Labs package drawing couldn't be confirmed.

mcus.name: EFR32MG21
mcus.description: High-performance 2.4 GHz Zigbee/Thread/BLE SoC with an 80 MHz Cortex-M33 and +20 dBm PA in a small QFN32. The chip behind many Zigbee/Thread USB coordinators.
notes: Only one package: QFN32 4x4 mm, 20 GPIO. A020 parts have the +20 dBm PA, A010 +10 dBm; 'B' parts add Secure Vault High.
Popular as a Zigbee/Thread coordinator or RCP (Home Assistant SkyConnect/ZBT-1, Sonoff ZBDongle-E) running EmberZNet/OpenThread RCP firmware.
Sleep current (about 5 µA EM2) is much higher than MG24/BG22, so it's a poor choice for coin-cell end devices.
Serial: 3 USART (UART/SPI/I2S) + 2 I2C; 4 timers. No DAC, no PDM, no USB.
Matter is set false conservatively: Silicon Labs' Matter SDK targets MG24/MG26 (MG21's 96 KB RAM is tight).
No ROM UART bootloader. Flash over SWD; the Gecko Bootloader (UART XMODEM/OTA) is optional and lives in flash.
Exposed-pad size isn't listed because the Silicon Labs package drawing couldn't be confirmed.

mcus.name: EFM8BB1
mcus.description: Tiny, cheap 25 MHz 8051 with 8 KB flash, 12-bit ADC and comparators in SOIC16/QSOP24/QFN20. Good for simple control jobs if you are comfortable with 8051 C.

ecosystem.vendorSdk: Simplicity Studio (8051 SDK, Keil C51) / SDCC

notes: Only 512 bytes of RAM (256 B internal + 256 B XRAM). ramKB shows 0 because the schema counts whole KB.

Programmed and debugged over Silicon Labs' 2-wire C2 interface (RSTb/C2CK + P2.0/C2D). You need a Silicon Labs USB Debug Adapter, a dev kit's on-board debugger or an open-source C2 programmer. Some EFM8 parts ship with a factory UART bootloader (AN945), but that isn't assumed here.
Peripherals: 1 UART, 1 SPI, 1 SMBus/I2C, 4 general 16-bit timers, a 3-channel PCA (PWM/capture), 2 comparators, 12-bit ADC (P0/P1 pins) and a temperature sensor.
Supply is 2.2-3.6 V only; the EFM8UB families add an on-chip 5 V regulator.
No Arduino/PlatformIO support. Use Keil C51 (free license through Simplicity Studio) or SDCC. Used in the Sonoff RF Bridge R2, so community firmware exists.
The 2 KB/4 KB (F2/F4) parts are cheaper; 'I' temperature-grade parts are rated to +125 °C.

mcus.name: STM32C011
mcus.description: ST's cheapest 32-bit MCU: 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 32 KB flash in SO-8 or TSSOP-20, a modern drop-in for 8-bit parts.
notes: No USB, no CAN, no DAC; 2 USART, 1 I2C, 1 SPI/I2S.
SO-8 version has only 6 usable I/Os (pins are multi-bonded).
Runs from 2.0-3.6 V only (not 5 V) despite targeting 8-bit replacement; I/Os are 5 V tolerant.
Internal 48 MHz RC (HSI48) means no crystal is needed.
Low-power is modest: Standby about 7.5 uA (RTC off in Standby/Shutdown), Shutdown 19 nA; ROM bootloader is USART/I2C.

mcus.name: STM32C031
mcus.description: Low-cost 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 32 KB flash and 12 KB RAM in TSSOP-20 to LQFP-48; a cheap general-purpose 32-bit replacement for 8-bit MCUs.
notes: No USB, CAN or DAC; 2 USART, 1 I2C, 1 SPI/I2S.
ADC external channels: 19 on LQFP48, 16 on LQFP32, 13 on TSSOP20.
Internal 48 MHz RC means no crystal is needed; supply is 2.0-3.6 V (5 V tolerant I/Os).

mcus.name: STM32C071
mcus.description: Low-cost 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 128 KB flash and crystal-less USB FS device/host; a cheap way to add native USB to a small design.
notes: USB 2.0 FS device and host; crystal-less operation (HSI48 + clock recovery) works in device mode only.
ROM bootloader supports USB DFU plus USART/I2C/SPI.
Only 2 USARTs and no CAN; consider the C092 for FDCAN or G0B1 for more UARTs.
Part numbers ending in N have a VDDIO2 pin (one fewer GPIO).

mcus.name: STM32C092
mcus.description: Cheapest STM32 with CAN-FD: 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 256 KB flash, one FDCAN and 4 USARTs, even in TSSOP-20.
notes: One FDCAN controller (needs an external CAN transceiver); 30 KB RAM because 6 KB is used as FDCAN message RAM (the CAN-less C091 has 36 KB).
No USB (see STM32C071) and no DAC.
The ROM bootloader supports FDCAN except on the TSSOP-20 package.

mcus.name: STM32F030
mcus.description: Long-running 48 MHz Cortex-M0 value line; dirt cheap and well documented, with up to 256 KB flash and 6 USARTs on the larger parts.
notes: Needs 2.4-3.6 V (higher minimum than most STM32s).
Peripheral count scales with memory: x4/x6 have 1 USART, 1 I2C, 1 SPI; x8 has 2/2/2; xC has 6 USART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI.
No USB, CAN, DAC or I2S; RTC without VBAT backup domain.

mcus.name: STM32F042
mcus.description: Small 48 MHz Cortex-M0 with crystal-less USB FS device, CAN and a USB DFU bootloader in TSSOP-20; a classic for USB-CAN adapters and tiny USB gadgets.
notes: USB FS device runs crystal-less from HSI48 + CRS; ROM bootloader supports USB DFU.
SPI2 only on the 48-pin package; HDMI-CEC included.
USB and bxCAN share a 1 KB packet SRAM (768 B left for USB when CAN is clocked); CAN is classic, not FD.

mcus.name: STM32F072
mcus.description: 48 MHz Cortex-M0 with 128 KB flash, crystal-less USB FS device, CAN, 2-channel DAC and 24 touch channels; widely used in USB keyboards and adapters.
notes: USB FS device runs crystal-less from HSI48 + CRS; ROM bootloader supports USB DFU.
4 USART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI (both I2S-capable), classic bxCAN, HDMI-CEC, 2 comparators.
USB and CAN share a 1 KB packet SRAM (768 B left for USB when CAN is clocked).

mcus.name: STM32F103
mcus.description: The classic 72 MHz Cortex-M3 of the "Blue Pill": cheap, everywhere, huge community; has USB FS device and CAN but is dated versus G0/G4/F4.
notes: USB (device only) and CAN share a 512-byte SRAM and cannot be used at the same time; USB needs a 1.5 kOhm D+ pull-up (many Blue Pills ship with the wrong 10k).
No USB DFU in ROM: flash via SWD or the USART1 bootloader (BOOT0), or install a USB bootloader such as STM32duino/HID.
C8/CB: 3 USART, 2 SPI (no I2S), no SDIO/DAC; high-density RC/ZE add 2 UARTs, SPI3, 2x I2S, SDIO, 2-channel DAC; FSMC (8080 LCD) only on 100/144-pin.
Many cheap boards carry clones/counterfeits (CKS32, CS32, APM32, GD32, CH32F103) instead of genuine ST parts.

mcus.name: STM32F303
mcus.description: 72 MHz Cortex-M4F with strong analog: 4 fast 12-bit ADCs, comparators, op-amps and DAC, plus USB FS device and CAN.
notes: RAM figures include CCM RAM: xB 32+8 KB, xC 40+8 KB, xE 64+16 KB.
UART4/5 only on 64-pin and larger; 48-pin parts have 3 USART and 2 I2C; the third I2C is xD/xE only.
USB is FS device only (no crystal-less mode, needs HSE); bxCAN is classic, not FD.
The small F303x6/x8 (e.g. K8T6) is a different subfamily: no USB, 2 ADCs, 3 DAC channels.

mcus.name: STM32F401
mcus.description: Entry-level 84 MHz Cortex-M4F with up to 512 KB flash and USB OTG FS; the chip on the cheap "Black Pill" boards.
notes: 48-pin (UFQFPN48) parts have no SDIO and only 10 ADC inputs; SPI4 exists only on 100-pin packages.
F401xB/xC parts (e.g. CCU6) have only 64 KB RAM.
USB OTG FS needs an accurate clock: use an HSE crystal for reliable USB.
No CAN, no DAC; 3 USART, 3 I2C.

mcus.name: STM32F411
mcus.description: 100 MHz Cortex-M4F with 512 KB flash, 128 KB RAM, USB OTG FS and five SPI/I2S; the popular "Black Pill" upgrade with broad Arduino/MicroPython support.
notes: All 5 SPIs can act as I2S (2 full-duplex), and SDIO is available even on the 48-pin package.
No CAN, no DAC, no Ethernet; 3 USART, 3 I2C.
USB OTG FS needs an HSE crystal for reliable USB timing.

mcus.name: STM32F405
mcus.description: Classic 168 MHz Cortex-M4F with 1 MB flash, 192 KB RAM, 2x CAN, USB OTG FS + HS and SDIO; powers the pyboard, Adafruit Feather STM32F405 and many flight controllers.
notes: 192 KB RAM includes 64 KB CCM RAM (CPU-only, not DMA accessible).
USB OTG_HS runs at full speed with its internal PHY; 480 Mbit/s needs an external ULPI PHY.
4 USART + 2 UART; classic bxCAN (not CAN-FD); no Ethernet or camera (see F407).
FSMC (parallel 8080 LCD / SRAM / NOR) only on 100-pin and larger packages.
No crypto accelerator (only RNG); the STM32F415 adds AES/HASH.

mcus.name: STM32F407
mcus.description: The STM32F405 plus 10/100 Ethernet MAC and camera interface: 168 MHz Cortex-M4F, 1 MB flash, 2x CAN, USB OTG FS + HS; very common on cheap dev boards.
notes: 192 KB RAM includes 64 KB CCM RAM (CPU-only, not DMA accessible).
Ethernet needs an external PHY (e.g. LAN8720 over RMII).
USB OTG_HS runs at full speed with its internal PHY; 480 Mbit/s needs an external ULPI PHY.
4 USART + 2 UART; classic bxCAN (not CAN-FD); FSMC usable as an 8080 parallel LCD interface.
No crypto accelerator (only RNG); the STM32F417 adds AES/HASH.

mcus.name: STM32F446
mcus.description: 180 MHz Cortex-M4F with 512 KB flash, 2x CAN, USB OTG FS + HS, Quad-SPI, SAI audio and camera interface; a fast all-rounder found on NUCLEO-F446RE.
notes: I2C count = 3 standard I2C + 1 FMPI2C (Fast-mode Plus).
USB OTG_HS runs at full speed with its internal PHY; 480 Mbit/s needs an external ULPI PHY.
4 USART + 2 UART; classic bxCAN (not CAN-FD); no Ethernet.
LQFP64 loses SPI4 and FMC and has a limited Quad-SPI; FMC on LQFP100 is Bank1 only (8080 LCD/SRAM, no SDRAM); full FMC on 144-pin.
No RNG and no crypto.

mcus.name: STM32F722
mcus.description: Budget 216 MHz Cortex-M7 with 512 KB flash, 256 KB RAM, USB OTG FS + HS, 2x SDMMC and Quad-SPI; popular in flight controllers.
notes: No Ethernet, no LTDC and no camera interface (see F746/F767).
USB OTG_HS needs an external ULPI PHY for 480 Mbit/s; the STM32F723 has an internal HS PHY.
4 USART + 4 UART on 100/144-pin (4 + 2 on LQFP64); SPI: 3 on LQFP64, 4 on LQFP100, 5 on LQFP144; SDMMC2 not on LQFP64.
One classic bxCAN (not CAN-FD); 256 KB RAM = 176 KB SRAM1 + 16 KB SRAM2 + 64 KB DTCM, plus 16 KB ITCM.
No crypto accelerator (the STM32F732 adds AES).

mcus.name: STM32F767
mcus.description: 216 MHz Cortex-M7 with double-precision FPU, 2 MB flash, 512 KB RAM, Ethernet, 3x CAN, USB HS/FS, LCD-TFT, camera and JPEG codec.
notes: 4 USART + 4 UART; 3 classic bxCAN (not CAN-FD); 6 SPI on 144/176-pin (fewer on LQFP100).
512 KB RAM = 368 KB SRAM1 + 16 KB SRAM2 + 128 KB DTCM, plus 16 KB ITCM; FMC supports SDRAM (Bank1 only on LQFP100).
USB OTG_HS needs an external ULPI PHY for 480 Mbit/s (internal FS PHY).
Ethernet needs an external PHY (MII/RMII).
No crypto accelerator (the STM32F777 adds AES/HASH).

mcus.name: STM32G030
mcus.description: Bare-bones 64 MHz Cortex-M0+ value line with up to 64 KB flash; very cheap and popular as a small helper MCU.
notes: Value line: no LPUART, no LPTIM, no DAC, no USB/CAN; 2.0-3.6 V supply (the G031 goes down to 1.7 V).
2 USART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI (one with I2S).
No Shutdown mode; ROM bootloader is USART/I2C only.
Internal 16 MHz RC + PLL reaches 64 MHz without a crystal.

mcus.name: STM32G031
mcus.description: Cheap 64 MHz Cortex-M0+ with up to 64 KB flash, LPUART, low-power timers and RTC, from SO-8 to LQFP-48.
notes: 2 USART + 1 LPUART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI (one with I2S), 2 LPTIM; no USB/CAN/DAC.
SO-8 (J) version has only 6 I/Os.
ROM bootloader is USART/I2C only.
Internal 16 MHz RC + PLL reaches 64 MHz without a crystal.

mcus.name: STM32G071
mcus.description: 64 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 128 KB flash, two USB Type-C Power Delivery (UCPD) controllers, 2-channel DAC and 5 UARTs; ideal for USB-C PD sinks/sources.
notes: UCPD provides Type-C CC handling/PD PHY only; there is no USB data controller (use G0B1 or C071 for USB).
Standard-pinout 28/32-pin parts expose only one UCPD port with one CC line; N-suffix parts have full dual UCPD but lose a GPIO.
4 USART + 1 LPUART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI (one with I2S), HDMI-CEC; no CAN.
36 KB SRAM without parity (32 KB with parity).

mcus.name: STM32G0B1
mcus.description: Feature-packed 64 MHz Cortex-M0+: up to 512 KB flash, 144 KB RAM, 2x CAN-FD, crystal-less USB device/host, USB-C PD and 8 UARTs; great value for CAN/USB gadgets.
notes: 144 KB SRAM without parity, 128 KB with parity enabled.
6 USART + 2 LPUART, 3 I2C, 3 SPI (2 with I2S), 2 FDCAN, 2 UCPD (only 1 port on standard-pinout 32-pin parts).
No HSE crystal oscillator on 32-pin packages; USB then runs crystal-less from HSI48 + CRS.
ROM bootloader supports USB DFU and FDCAN as well as USART/I2C/SPI.
Popular in 3D-printer CAN toolhead boards (Klipper) and USB-C PD sinks.

mcus.name: STM32G431
mcus.description: 170 MHz Cortex-M4F mixed-signal MCU with CAN-FD, USB FS, UCPD, CORDIC/FMAC math accelerators and fast analog; a favourite for motor control and power conversion.
notes: 32 KB SRAM = 16 KB SRAM1 + 6 KB SRAM2 + 10 KB CCM SRAM.
No Quad-SPI and no FMC on the G431 (G474/G491 have Quad-SPI).
UART counts depend on package: 3 USART + UART4 + LPUART on 64-pin and larger, 3 USART + LPUART on 48-pin, 2 USART + LPUART on 32-pin.
2 ADCs (up to 23 channels), 4 DAC channels of which 2 are external outputs, 4 comparators, 3 op-amps.
USB is full-speed device only; crystal-less USB is only rated from -15 to 85 C.

mcus.name: STM32G474
mcus.description: 170 MHz Cortex-M4F with a 184 ps high-resolution timer (HRTIM), 5 ADCs, 7 DACs, 3x CAN-FD, Quad-SPI and USB FS; the go-to for digital power and advanced motor control.
notes: HRTIM: 6 x 16-bit counters, 184 ps resolution, 12 PWM outputs.
128 KB SRAM = 80 KB SRAM1 + 16 KB SRAM2 + 32 KB CCM SRAM.
5 x 12-bit ADCs (up to 42 channels on 100-pin); 7 DAC channels, 3 of them external outputs; 7 comparators, 6 op-amps.
3 USART + 2 UART + 1 LPUART on 64-pin and larger (48-pin has no UARTs 4/5); 4th SPI and FMC (8080 LCD/SRAM) only on 80/100/128-pin parts.
USB is full-speed device only.

mcus.name: STM32G491
mcus.description: Mid-range 170 MHz Cortex-M4F with 512 KB flash, 2x CAN-FD, Quad-SPI, 3 ADCs and USB FS; more memory than the G431 without the G474 price.
notes: 112 KB SRAM = 80 KB SRAM1 + 16 KB SRAM2 + 16 KB CCM SRAM.
3 USART + 2 UART + 1 LPUART on 64-pin and larger; 48-pin has no UART4/5.
3 x 12-bit ADCs (up to 36 channels on 100-pin); 2 external DAC channels; no HRTIM (see G474).
USB is full-speed device only.

mcus.name: STM32H503
mcus.description: Low-cost 250 MHz Cortex-M33 with 128 KB flash, CAN-FD, USB FS, I3C and a 2-channel DAC; lots of speed for small control tasks.
notes: No TrustZone on the H503 (unlike H56x/H57x); has HASH (SHA-2) and TRNG but no AES/PKA.
3 USART + 1 LPUART; 2 I2C plus 2 I3C that share pins with the I2C buses.
Not a low-power part: Standby with RTC is about 3.3 uA and there is no Shutdown mode.
ROM bootloader supports USB DFU, FDCAN, USART, I2C, I3C and SPI.

mcus.name: STM32H563
mcus.description: Fast 250 MHz Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, 2 MB flash, 640 KB RAM, Ethernet, 2x CAN-FD, USB-C PD and Octo-SPI; a modern replacement for F4/F7 designs.
notes: Up to 6 USART + 6 UART + 1 LPUART on 144/176-pin parts (5+5+1 on LQFP64); also 1x I3C.
Has HASH (SHA-2), PKA and TrustZone; the AES/SAES cipher engines are only on the STM32H573.
GPIO count is lower on SMPS (Q-suffix) parts, e.g. 110 instead of 112 on LQFP144.
USB is full-speed only (host + device) with a UCPD Type-C/PD controller; 1 Gbit Ethernet is not supported (10/100 MAC).
No LTDC; displays connect via the FMC (8080 parallel, not on LQFP64), SPI or DCMI/PSSI.
Some smaller-package ordering codes (H562) have fewer FDCAN/SDMMC instances; check the datasheet table.

mcus.name: STM32H723
mcus.description: Cheapest 550 MHz Cortex-M7: 1 MB flash, 564 KB RAM, 3x CAN-FD, Ethernet, 2x Octo-SPI and LCD-TFT in hand-solderable LQFP packages.
notes: Single USB OTG controller: full-speed with on-chip PHY; high-speed needs an external ULPI PHY.
RAM = 128 KB DTCM + 432 KB system RAM (192 KB shareable with ITCM) + 4 KB backup.
Two 16-bit ADCs plus one 12-bit ADC; 5 USART + 5 UART + 1 LPUART.
LQFP100 parts have only one usable Octo-SPI port (two on 144-pin) and 5 SPIs instead of 6.
No crypto accelerator (that is the STM32H733).

mcus.name: STM32H743
mcus.description: Classic 480 MHz Cortex-M7 workhorse with 2 MB flash, 1 MB RAM, Ethernet, 2x CAN-FD, USB HS/FS, LCD-TFT and camera interface; widely used in flight controllers.
notes: "1 MB" RAM = 192 KB TCM (64 KB ITCM + 128 KB DTCM) + 864 KB SRAM split across domains + 4 KB backup; not one contiguous block.
USB OTG_HS (on-chip FS PHY, external ULPI PHY for 480 Mbit/s) + USB OTG_FS.
4 USART + 4 UART + 1 LPUART; three 16-bit ADCs; JPEG codec and Chrom-ART on chip.
FMC supports SDRAM/SRAM/NOR/NAND for large external frame buffers.
Early silicon (rev Y) was limited to 400 MHz; rev V parts run at 480 MHz.

mcus.name: STM32H747
mcus.description: Dual-core 480 MHz Cortex-M7 + 240 MHz Cortex-M4 with 2 MB flash, 1 MB RAM, MIPI-DSI display, Ethernet and USB HS; the chip in Arduino Portenta H7 and GIGA R1.
notes: Cortex-M7 at 480 MHz plus Cortex-M4 at 240 MHz sharing the same peripherals.
MIPI-DSI host + LTDC; USB OTG_HS (ULPI for 480 Mbit/s) + OTG_FS.
Needs SMPS/LDO supply configuration set correctly in firmware; a wrong setting can lock the chip until a special recovery.
LQFP176/208 pinouts are not compatible with the single-core H743; TFBGA265 (TFBGA240+25) ballout is mostly compatible.
GPIO depends heavily on package: 119 (LQFP176), 148 (LQFP208), 168 (TFBGA265).

mcus.name: STM32L031
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 32 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 32 KB flash, LPUART and EEPROM; sips sub-microamp currents in coin-cell sensor nodes.
notes: 1 USART + 1 LPUART, 1 I2C, 1 SPI; no USB, CAN or DAC.
Includes 1 KB of true data EEPROM.
Max clock is only 32 MHz.

mcus.name: STM32L432
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 80 MHz Cortex-M4F in a tiny 32-pin package with CAN, crystal-less USB, Quad-SPI and DAC; the NUCLEO-L432KC chip.
notes: 2 USART + 1 LPUART, 2 I2C, 2 SPI; audio via SAI (no I2S peripheral).
USB is full-speed device only, crystal-less via HSI48 + CRS; there is no separate VDDUSB pin, so USB needs VDD around 3.3 V.
Only available in 32-pin UFQFPN (and WLCSP).

mcus.name: STM32L476
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 80 MHz Cortex-M4F with 1 MB flash, USB OTG FS, segment LCD driver, SDMMC, Quad-SPI and CAN; a flexible low-power workhorse.
notes: 128 KB SRAM = 96 KB SRAM1 + 32 KB SRAM2 (SRAM2 can be retained in Standby).
3 USART + 2 UART + 1 LPUART; audio via 2x SAI (no I2S peripheral).
Segment LCD driver up to 8x40 (8x28 on LQFP64) with internal step-up converter; touch channels 12 / 21 / 24 on 64 / 100 / 144-pin.
No HSI48: USB OTG FS needs an HSE crystal or LSE-trimmed MSI; VDDUSB is a separate 3.0-3.6 V supply.
FMC (static memories / 8080 LCD) only on 100-pin and larger packages.

mcus.name: STM32U031
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 56 MHz Cortex-M0+ (160 nA standby with RTC) with 64 KB flash, 6 UARTs and capacitive touch; for battery-powered sensors.
notes: 4 USART + 2 LPUART, 3 I2C, 2 SPI (no I2S); no USB or segment LCD (see STM32U073/U083).
Standby with RTC is 0.16 uA at 1.8 V (about 0.24 uA at 3 V); shutdown 16 nA.
Touch channels: 12 on LQFP48, 7 on UFQFPN32, 3 on TSSOP20.

mcus.name: STM32U575
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 160 MHz Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, 2 MB flash and 786 KB RAM, CAN-FD, USB OTG with Type-C PD, 2x Octo-SPI and a 14-bit ADC.
notes: 786 KB SRAM with ECC off (722 KB with ECC on).
One 14-bit ADC + one 12-bit ADC (autonomous in Stop 2); 3 USART + 2 UART + 1 LPUART.
HASH accelerator and TrustZone; AES/SAES/PKA/OTFDEC are only on the STM32U585.
No I2S peripheral (audio via 2x SAI); the 48-pin package has no SDMMC, DCMI or UART5.
No LTDC; FMC (8080 parallel LCD/SRAM/PSRAM) is available on 100-pin and larger packages.
Q-suffix part numbers include the SMPS step-down converter (needs an external inductor).

mcus.name: STM32U585
mcus.description: STM32U575 plus hardware AES/SAES, PKA and on-the-fly external memory decryption; the secure ultra-low-power Cortex-M33 used in ST IoT reference designs.
notes: Adds AES, SAES (side-channel resistant), PKA and OTFDEC over the U575; otherwise identical peripherals.
One 14-bit ADC + one 12-bit ADC; 3 USART + 2 UART + 1 LPUART; no I2S (use SAI).
Targets PSA Certified Level 3 / SESIP3 designs; used on the B-U585I-IOT02A Discovery kit.
Q-suffix part numbers include the SMPS step-down converter (needs an external inductor).

mcus.name: STM32WB55
mcus.description: Bluetooth LE + 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee/Matter) dual-core MCU: 64 MHz Cortex-M4 for the app, Cortex-M0+ for the radio, 1 MB flash, USB FS and a mature ST stack.
notes: Radio stack runs on the Cortex-M0+ and must be flashed as an encrypted ST binary via the FUS; it occupies part of the 1 MB flash/256 KB RAM.
Requires a 32 MHz HSE crystal; the embedded SMPS needs an external inductor.
UFQFPN48 (C) parts: 1 SPI, 10 ADC inputs, no touch sensing, 4x13 segment LCD; VFQFPN68 (R) parts: 2 SPI, 16 ADC inputs, 6 touch channels.
Single USART + LPUART; USB is full-speed device only (crystal-less); ROM bootloader supports USB DFU.
Datasheet lists Bluetooth 5.3; newer ST stacks add Bluetooth 5.4 features.

mcus.name: STM32WBA55
mcus.description: Single-core 100 MHz Cortex-M33 wireless MCU for Bluetooth LE, Thread, Zigbee and Matter with TrustZone, SESIP3 security and very low radio current.
notes: No USB on the WBA5x (the newer WBA6x adds USB OTG HS).
+10 dBm max TX power; external PA support; Bluetooth LE Audio (Auracast) capable. ST now also advertises Bluetooth LE 6.0 with recent stacks.
Radio stack runs on the same Cortex-M33 as the application (no separate radio core like WB55).
2 USART + 1 LPUART, 2x I2C, 2x SPI, 1x SAI; AES, SAES, PKA, HASH and TrustZone.
Needs a 32 MHz HSE crystal; SMPS variants need an external inductor.

mcus.name: STM32WL55
mcus.description: LoRa / sub-GHz SoC with dual Cortex-M4 + M0+ cores, 256 KB flash and a 150-960 MHz radio (LoRa, (G)FSK, BPSK) with up to +22 dBm output.
notes: Second core (Cortex-M0+) lets the LoRaWAN stack run separately from the application.
Needs a 32 MHz TCXO or crystal and an RF matching network for the high-power (+22 dBm) and/or low-power (+15 dBm) PA outputs.
No USB: program over SWD or the UART/SPI ROM bootloader.
2 USART + 1 LPUART, 3x I2C, 2x SPI (one with I2S); AES-256, PKA and TRNG.

mcus.name: STM32WLE5
mcus.description: Single-core Cortex-M4 LoRa / sub-GHz SoC (150-960 MHz, up to +22 dBm); the chip inside popular modules like Seeed LoRa-E5 and RAK3172.
notes: Needs a 32 MHz TCXO or crystal and RF matching; many designs use a pre-certified module (LoRa-E5, RAK3172) instead.
No USB: program over SWD or the UART/SPI ROM bootloader.
WLE5 includes the AES-256 accelerator; the cheaper WLE4 does not.
2 USART + 1 LPUART, 3x I2C, 2x SPI (one with I2S), 1-channel DAC.

mcus.name: STM32N657
mcus.description: Edge-AI MCU: 800 MHz Cortex-M55 with Helium plus a 600 GOPS Neural-ART NPU, 4.2 MB SRAM, MIPI CSI-2 camera + ISP, H.264 encoder, Gigabit Ethernet and 2x USB HS.
notes: No internal flash: code boots from external XSPI NOR flash (secure boot ROM loads it into SRAM or runs XIP).
Only BGA packages (smallest pitch 0.5 mm on VFBGA142/223); VFBGA264 at 0.8 mm is the easiest to route.
Smaller packages lose peripherals: VFBGA142 (Z0) has no SDMMC, 2 USART + 3 UART and no 16-bit XSPI.
Two USB 2.0 OTG HS controllers with on-chip HS PHYs (one with UCPD); 5 USART + 5 UART + 1 LPUART, 2x I3C.
N657 includes crypto (AES/SAES/PKA/MCE); the N647 is the same chip without the NPU.

mcus.name: MSPM0C1104
mcus.description: Tiny 24 MHz Cortex-M0+ for sub-$0.50 jobs: 16 KB flash, 12-bit ADC and timers in packages down to SOT-23-8 and a 1.6 mm WCSP; great for replacing 8-bit MCUs.
notes: Very small memory: 16 KB flash and only 1 KB SRAM.
No ROM bootloader (BSL) on the C-series: blank chips must be flashed over SWD (XDS110, J-Link or CMSIS-DAP with OpenOCD/pyOCD).
Internal oscillators only (24 MHz SYSOSC, 32 kHz LFOSC); no crystal, RTC, comparator or DAC.
8-pin packages (SOT-23-8, WSON-8, WCSP) expose only 6 GPIO; the 20-pin VSSOP gives 18. The 20-pin TSSOP is sold as MSPS003F4, not MSPM0C1104.
PWM count (14) is TI's figure and includes the advanced timer's complementary outputs.
No mature Rust HAL yet (embassy MSPM0 support is still in development).

mcus.name: MSPM0L1306
mcus.description: Low-power 32 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 64 KB flash, 1.68 Msps 12-bit ADC and two zero-drift op-amps; a cheap analog sensor front-end with a ROM UART/I2C bootloader.
notes: Only 4 KB SRAM.
ROM bootstrap loader (BSL) over UART or I2C, invoked with the BSL pin at reset, so no programmer is strictly needed.
No RTC peripheral, no DAC output and no crystal oscillator (internal ±1.2% SYSOSC and 32 kHz LFOSC only). STANDBY figure is with a 32 kHz timer running.
Analog extras: 2 zero-drift chopper op-amps with PGA, 1 general-purpose amp, 1 fast comparator with 8-bit reference DAC.
No upstream Zephyr board and no mature Rust HAL yet.

mcus.name: MSPM0G3507
mcus.description: 80 MHz Cortex-M0+ with CAN-FD, two 4 Msps 12-bit ADCs, DAC, comparators and op-amps for about $1-3; a cheap pick for motor control and CAN-FD nodes.
notes: One MCAN controller supporting CAN 2.0 A/B and CAN-FD; needs an external transceiver (an HFXT crystal is advisable for CAN bit timing).
ROM bootstrap loader (BSL) over UART or I2C.
Analog: 2 simultaneous-sampling 4 Msps ADCs (17 external channels on LQFP-64), 1 Msps 12-bit DAC, 3 comparators, 2 zero-drift op-amps, 1 GPAMP; math accelerator (DIV/SQRT/MAC/TRIG).
AES-128/256, TRNG and CRC; RTC with calendar; STANDBY figure is with LFXT and RTC running.
Upstream Zephyr board lp_mspm0g3507 exists, but driver coverage is still growing. Rust support (embassy) is not released yet.
Cheap WeAct MSPM0G3507 core board (VQFN-32 part) is available for a few dollars.

mcus.name: MSP430FR2433
mcus.description: Ultra-low-power 16-bit MSP430 with 15.5 KB FRAM (fast, high-endurance non-volatile memory) and ~1 µA sleep with RTC; good for coin-cell sensors and data logging.
notes: 15.5 KB FRAM total (15 KB program + 512 B information memory); listed as 15 KB here.
Serial: eUSCI_A0/A1 each do UART or SPI, eUSCI_B0 does I2C or SPI. So max 2 UART, 1 I2C or 3 SPI, but they share the same 3 modules.
Only 4 PWM outputs reach pins (TA0.1/2, TA1.1/2); Timer_A2/A3 instances have no external outputs.
RTC is a 16-bit counter-only RTC (no calendar). Sleep figure is LPM3 with RTC and RAM retained; LPM3.5 drops to 0.73 µA (no RAM retention).
ROM BSL over UART or I2C needs an entry sequence on RST/TEST (blank devices enter it automatically).
Only VQFN-24 and DSBGA packages. Energia (Arduino-like) is discontinued; the PlatformIO timsp430 platform still supports the MSP-EXP430FR2433 LaunchPad.

mcus.name: MSP430G2553
mcus.description: Classic low-power 16-bit MCU in a breadboard-friendly DIP-20; the chip from the MSP-EXP430G2 LaunchPad, ideal for learning and very simple battery gadgets.
notes: Only 512 bytes of SRAM (stored as ramKB 0 because the schema uses whole KB).
One USCI_A (UART/LIN/IrDA or SPI) and one USCI_B (I2C or SPI): 1 UART + 1 I2C, or up to 2 SPI if you give those up.
No RTC peripheral (use Timer_A with a 32 kHz crystal). PWM: 2x Timer_A3 give 4 usable PWM outputs.
Capacitive touch on any GPIO via the pin-oscillator (no dedicated touch hardware).
ROM BSL on P1.1 (TX) / P1.5 (RX) needs a special RST/TEST entry sequence; most people flash via a LaunchPad's eZ-FET over Spy-Bi-Wire.
Energia (Arduino-like) is discontinued; the PlatformIO timsp430 platform still supports the G2553 LaunchPad.

mcus.name: CC2340R5
mcus.description: Low-cost 48 MHz Cortex-M0+ Bluetooth LE 5.4 SoC (also Zigbee and Thread) with 512 KB flash, under 1 µA standby and roughly $1-2 pricing.
notes: No USB and no I2S; only 1 UART, 1 I2C and 1 SPI.
CC2340R52 has 36 KB SRAM, CC2340R53 has 64 KB (same 512 KB flash). Standby figure is for the R52 with RTC and full RAM retention.
Qualified against Bluetooth Core 5.4 (older listings say 5.3). Zigbee via the F3 SDK, Thread via TI's OpenThread SDK; no Matter support.
Max TX power +8 dBm; needs a 48 MHz crystal. QFN-24 version exposes only 12 GPIO.
ROM serial bootloader over UART or SPI.
Third-party module: RF-star RF-BM-2340A2 (CC2340R52 in QFN-24, LCSC C20624105, about $4).

mcus.name: CC2652R
mcus.description: 48 MHz Cortex-M4F multiprotocol 2.4 GHz SoC for Zigbee, Thread and BLE 5.2 with a low-power sensor controller; a well-proven Zigbee/Thread workhorse.
notes: Not a Matter part: TI's Matter support targets the larger-flash CC2652R7 / CC2674 devices.
Many popular Zigbee coordinator modules (Sonoff ZBDongle-P, Ebyte E72-2G4M20S1E) use the CC2652P (+20 dBm PA), not the CC2652R.
CC2652RSIP is TI's certified 7x7 mm system-in-package (crystals, balun and DC/DC parts inside) with 32 GPIO on a 73-pad LGA.
Autonomous 16-bit sensor controller (4 KB SRAM) for low-power sensing and capacitive touch; +5 dBm max TX.
ROM serial bootloader over UART or SPI; debug is 2-pin cJTAG by default (XDS110).
LCSC rarely stocks it (listed at broker prices); buy from DigiKey/Mouser.

mcus.name: CC1352P
mcus.description: Dual-band Sub-1 GHz + 2.4 GHz Cortex-M4F SoC with an integrated +20 dBm PA: long-range sub-GHz links plus Zigbee, Thread and BLE 5.2 on one chip.
notes: Integrated +20 dBm PA (63 mA at 915 MHz, 85 mA at 2.4 GHz); the RF matching network decides which band gets the high-power path (see LAUNCHXL-CC1352P1 vs -P-2).
Sub-GHz stacks: TI 15.4-Stack, Wi-SUN, Amazon Sidewalk, mioty, Wireless M-Bus, KNX RF; -121 dBm long-range mode. Not LoRa-compatible.
Not a Matter part (TI's Matter-capable dual-band chip is the CC1354P10).
26 GPIO (fewer than the CC1352R because PA pins are used).
Third-party modules: Ebyte E79-900DM2005S (868/915 MHz) and E79-400DM2005S (433 MHz), 32x20 mm.
ROM serial bootloader over UART or SPI; debug is 2-pin cJTAG by default.

mcus.name: CC3235S
mcus.description: Dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 4 SoC with an 80 MHz Cortex-M4 app core and an offloaded TCP/IP + TLS network processor; pick it when you need 5 GHz Wi-Fi.
notes: No internal flash: needs an external SPI serial flash (up to 32 MB) holding the file system; the app runs from the 256 KB SRAM. CC3235SF adds 1 MB on-chip flash.
No Bluetooth (only coexistence pins for an external 2.4 GHz radio). 802.11a/b/g/n, 2.4 + 5 GHz; peak TX current is about 223 mA.
ADC inputs max 1.5 V (pins tolerate 1.8 V); the SD host is 1-bit only.
Flashing is done over UART (SOP pins in UARTLOAD mode) with TI UniFlash; debug over JTAG/SWD.
Sleep figure is LPDS with 256 KB RAM retained; hibernate (RTC only) is 4.5 µA.
Zephyr only supports the CC3235SF variant. CC3235MODS module (CC3235MODSM2MOBR) is certified and includes 4 MB flash and crystals but needs an external antenna (CC3235MODAS has one built in).

mcus.name: TM4C123GH6PM
mcus.description: 80 MHz Cortex-M4F with lots of I/O: 8 UARTs, 4 I2C, 4 SPI, 2 CAN, USB OTG and 16 motor-control PWMs; the chip on the classic Tiva C LaunchPad.
notes: USB 2.0 full-speed OTG with internal PHY; two CAN 2.0 A/B controllers (no CAN-FD, external transceivers needed).
3.3 V only (3.15-3.63 V supply). 2 KB EEPROM; two 1 Msps ADCs sharing 12 inputs; 2 QEI.
PWM count is the two dedicated PWM modules (16 outputs); the 12 general-purpose timers can add more.
ROM boot loader (UART0, SSI0, I2C0, USB DFU) runs automatically on blank flash; afterwards only if a GPIO is set up in BOOTCFG.
Sleep figure is Hibernate with RTC (SRAM not retained; 16 battery-backed words). Deep-sleep with RAM retention is about 1 mA.
Pricey for an M4F today (about $14+). Energia is discontinued; PlatformIO titiva supports the EK-TM4C123GXL. Zephyr's ek_tm4c123gxl support is minimal and Rust (tm4c123x-hal) is community-maintained.

mcus.name: CH32V003
mcus.description: The famous 10-cent RISC-V MCU: 48 MHz, 16 KB flash, runs straight from 5 V, down to SOP-8; ideal for tiny glue logic and replacing 8-bit parts.
notes: No USB. Flash and debug use the 1-wire SWIO pin with a WCH-LinkE (~$4); ST-Link/J-Link do not work.
Has a factory UART bootloader (PD5/PD6, 115200 baud), but no BOOT pin: a blank chip boots straight into user flash, so you need a WCH-LinkE once to set START_MODE or flash an app that jumps to it.
Only 2 KB RAM and RV32EC (16 registers). ADC is 10-bit. One built-in op-amp/comparator.
ch32v003fun (bare-metal SDK) and rv003usb (bit-banged low-speed USB) are popular community projects.
Rated 2.7-5.5 V; I/O levels follow VDD, so it can talk 5 V logic when powered from 5 V.

mcus.name: CH32V006
mcus.description: Bigger brother of the CH32V003: 62 KB flash, 8 KB RAM, 12-bit ADC, two UARTs and touch keys, still 5 V tolerant supply and under $0.35.
notes: Part of the 2024 CH32V002/V004/V005/V006/V007 refresh (QingKe V2C). CH32V002 (16 KB/4 KB) is the ultra-cheap sibling; CH32V005 drops touch keys and TIM3.
Stock at LCSC/JLCPCB is still thin (Nov 2026); check availability before committing. TSSOP-20 price is from the JLCPCB parts library.
Debug: 1-wire SWIO by default, 2-wire optional; needs a WCH-LinkE. The 3.3 KB BOOT area holds a factory bootloader, but there is no BOOT pin, so plan on a WCH-LinkE for the first flash.
Datasheet is Chinese-first; English reference manual is shared with the CH32V00x family. Use MounRiver Studio or ch32v003fun-style toolchains.
ADC needs VDD >= 2.4 V. Has an op-amp with 3-way input polling.

mcus.name: CH32V203
mcus.description: Cheap 144 MHz RISC-V STM32F103 alternative with two USB controllers (device + host/OTG), CAN and 4 UARTs from about $0.65.
notes: Peripherals vary a lot by package: F6/G6 have only USBD (device) and 1-2 UARTs; F8 has only USBFS; C8 and RB have both USB controllers, 4 UARTs, 2 I2C, 2 SPI.
10 Mbit Ethernet MAC+PHY exists only on CH32V203RBT6.
Flash size in the part number is the zero-wait region; all parts have 224 KB total flash (the rest runs with wait states). RB can trade flash for up to 64 KB SRAM via option bytes.
CAN and USBD share a 512-byte buffer: both work together but USBD is then limited to 384 bytes.
Factory USB/UART ISP bootloader (BOOT0 pin). Debug is WCH 2-wire SDI via WCH-LinkE (not ARM SWD).
Runs 3.3 V only (2.4-3.6 V); most I/O are 5 V tolerant (FT).

mcus.name: CH32V305
mcus.description: Cheapest way to get USB 2.0 High-Speed with a built-in PHY, plus 2x CAN, SDIO and an FPU, in packages down to TSSOP-20.
notes: USB HS (480 Mbit/s) PHY is on-chip on every CH32V305. Only RB (LQFP-64) also has the full-speed USB host/device controller; FB/GB have USBHS only.
Package limits: FBP6 has 2 UARTs, 1 SPI, 1 CAN, no SDIO; GBU6 has 1 CAN and SDIO; RBT6 has 2 CAN and SDIO. No Ethernet (see CH32V307).
128 KB zero-wait flash; total flash 480 KB on 256 KB-class parts (CH32V305CCT6, rarely stocked).
Debug is WCH 2-wire SDI via WCH-LinkE (not ARM SWD). Factory USB/UART ISP bootloader via BOOT0.

mcus.name: CH32V307
mcus.description: Feature-packed 144 MHz RISC-V with FPU: USB HS with PHY + USB FS OTG, Ethernet with built-in 10M PHY, 2x CAN, SDIO, camera port and 8 UARTs for about $3.
notes: Ethernet: Gigabit MAC with an on-chip 10 Mbit PHY; 100M/1G needs an external PHY (RMII/RGMII).
USB HS (480 Mbit/s) PHY is on-chip, plus a separate USB FS OTG controller.
256 KB zero-wait flash out of 480 KB total; option bytes can trade flash for up to 128 KB SRAM (e.g. 192 KB flash + 128 KB RAM).
FSMC (8080 LCD / external SRAM) only on the LQFP-100 part. DVP camera interface is listed for CH32V307 only.
Debug is WCH 2-wire SDI via WCH-LinkE (not ARM SWD). Factory USB/UART ISP bootloader via BOOT0.

mcus.name: CH32X035
mcus.description: Low-cost RISC-V with USB FS host/device plus a built-in USB PD / Type-C controller and PHY, runs from 2-5.5 V; great for USB-C gadgets and PD sinks.
notes: USB is one full-speed controller (host OR device at a time). USB PD supports Source, Sink and DRP; 20-pin parts have USB device + PD only (no host).
Supply 2.0-5.5 V without USB/PD, 3.0-5.3 V when USB or PD is used; ADC needs >= 2.5 V. Internal 48 MHz oscillator, no crystal needed for USB.
Has a PIOC programmable protocol I/O co-processor (small 8-bit eMCU) for WS2812/1-wire style protocols; not comparable to RP2040 PIO.
No RTC. A 64-pin CH32X035R8T6 (60 GPIO, 14 ADC/touch) exists but is rarely stocked.
Factory bootloader over USB or UART: hold PC17 high at power-up. Debug is WCH 2-wire SDI via WCH-LinkE.

mcus.name: CH32L103
mcus.description: Probably the cheapest CAN-FD MCU (~$0.80): 96 MHz low-power RISC-V with USB FS host/device, USB PD/Type-C, 4 UARTs and sub-1 uA standby.
notes: CAN FD (up to 8 Mbit/s data phase) only on CH32L103C8T6 and CH32L103K8U6; other packages have classic CAN 2.0B.
K8U6/F8U6 have built-in 5.1k Rd resistors for Type-C sink. USB is one FS controller (host or device).
Small packages lose peripherals: K8U6/F8P6 have 1 SPI and 1 I2C.
Factory USB/UART (USART2) ISP bootloader via BOOT0. Debug is WCH 2-wire SDI via WCH-LinkE.
K8U6 was out of stock at LCSC when checked (Nov 2026).

mcus.name: CH552
mcus.description: Classic ~$0.55 8051 with native USB device and a factory USB bootloader; runs from 5 V with an internal 3.3 V regulator, down to MSOP-10.
notes: USB is device-only (full/low speed); CC pins support basic Type-C attach detection but no USB PD protocol.
16 KB flash (14 KB usable when the factory bootloader is kept), 256 B iRAM + 1 KB xRAM. No hardware I2C (bit-bang it). ADC is 8-bit.
No debugger: flash over USB/UART with WCHISPTool, wchisp or ch55xduino. Bootloader is entered by pulling UDP (or P1.5 on newer bootloaders) at power-up.
5 V mode: 3.7-5.5 V on VCC with V33 decoupled; 3.3 V mode: tie V33 to VCC (2.8-3.6 V). 24 MHz needs the 5 V supply.
Pin counts include RST, XI/XO and the USB pins. WCH now recommends CH543/CH548 for new designs and discourages CH552E.

mcus.name: CH582
mcus.description: Cheap BLE 5 RISC-V SoC with two USB FS host/device controllers, 448 KB flash, AES and sub-1 uA sleep for about $1.10.
notes: BLE only (datasheet: Bluetooth LE 5.0, 2M/1M/Coded PHY, +6 dBm). Needs a 32 MHz crystal; BLE stack is a closed-source WCH library.
448 KB code flash + 32 KB data flash; 32 KB SRAM (30 KB + 2 KB retained in sleep). Built-in DC-DC.
CH582F (QFN-28) has 20 GPIO, 8 ADC channels; CH582M (QFN-48) has 40 GPIO. CH583M adds a second SPI.
Factory USB/UART ISP bootloader; 2-wire debug (WCH-LinkE) must first be enabled via the ISP tool.
48-pin part has a fine 0.35 mm pitch.

mcus.name: CH592
mcus.description: Ultra-cheap BLE 5.4 RISC-V SoC (~$0.70) with USB FS host/device, segment-LCD driver, AES and 1.7 V operation; good for coin-cell BLE gadgets.
notes: BLE 5.4 (1M/2M PHY, +4.5 dBm, -95 dBm sensitivity). Needs a 32 MHz crystal; BLE stack is a closed-source WCH library.
Segment LCD driver up to 20x4 (CH592X). CH592A/CH591 are cut-down variants (no touch/I2C on CH591, 256 KB flash).
CH592D (QFN-20) has 12 GPIO and only 2 UARTs/4 ADC channels.
Factory USB/UART ISP bootloader; 2-wire debug (WCH-LinkE) must first be enabled via the ISP tool.

mcus.name: BL602/BL604
mcus.description: Very cheap 192 MHz RISC-V Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5.0 SoC with an FPU; an ESP8266-class alternative (e.g. Ai-WB2 modules) if you can live with a smaller ecosystem.
notes: BLE 5.0 without 2M PHY, Coded PHY or extended advertising.
Small ecosystem: no official Arduino or MicroPython; use the Bouffalo SDK or Zephyr (bl60x, Ai-WB2-12F kit).
SDIO is slave-only (no SD-card host); no I2S and no USB - flash over UART with the Bouffalo flasher (ROM UART/SDIO boot).
BL602C-00 has no internal flash and needs an external QSPI flash; the -20 parts have 2 MB in package.
Supply range 2.1-3.63 V per datasheet (VDDIO can run at 1.8 V); needs a 24/26/32/38.4/40 MHz crystal.
Ai-WB2-12F uses the ESP-12F outline (16x24 mm, 22 pads, 2 mm pitch) but its pinout differs.

mcus.name: BL616/BL618
mcus.description: 320 MHz RISC-V SoC with Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3 dual-mode and 802.15.4, plus USB 2.0 High-Speed, Ethernet, SD host, camera and display interfaces at a very low price.
notes: BL616 (QFN40) has 19 GPIO; BL618 (QFN56) has 35 GPIO. Ai-M62 modules use BL616, Ai-M61 modules use BL618.
Rare combination of Wi-Fi 6 + BT 5.3 dual-mode (Classic + LE) + 802.15.4 on one radio; BL616C ordering code lists Thread, BL618M lists Zigbee/Thread.
USB 2.0 HS OTG with on-chip PHY; ROM can download over UART (GPIO21/22), USB or SDIO (hold GPIO2 high at reset).
SD/MMC host, Ethernet RMII MAC, DVP camera, DBI/QSPI/RGB display, MJPEG encoder and a mono audio codec on chip.
SRAM is 532 KB including caches and 4 KB HBN RAM (480 KB general-purpose OCRAM+WRAM); 2.97-3.63 V supply (datasheet lists the UARTs as 'support 5V IO').

Small ecosystem: no official Arduino/MicroPython; use the Bouffalo SDK or Zephyr (bl61x, Ai-M61/M62 kits, Sipeed M0S dock). External flash limit is a conservative estimate (Ai-Thinker modules support up to 16 MB).

mcus.name: RTL8720DN
mcus.description: Dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5.0 SoC with a 200 MHz Cortex-M33-class core; the cheap BW16 module is the easiest way to get 5 GHz Wi-Fi in Arduino.
mcus.core: Real-M300 (Arm Cortex-M33 compatible, 200 MHz) + Real-M200 (Cortex-M23 compatible) low-power core
notes: Dual-band 802.11a/b/g/n (Wi-Fi 4, 2.4 + 5 GHz) and BLE 5.0 sharing one antenna.
RTL8720DN has no in-package flash or PSRAM (RTL8720DF adds 4 MB flash, RTL8721DM/RTL8722DM add 4 MB PSRAM); the BW16 module includes external flash.
Realtek's selection table lists one USB interface on the RTL8720DN, but BW16 does not break it out and the Arduino SDK doesn't use it - treated as unavailable here.
ADC and capacitive-touch share the same 3 pins; KM0 low-power core adds 64 KB SRAM (not counted).
Flash over the LOG UART (PA7/PA8) with the Ameba image tool or Arduino upload mode; debug via SWD (PB3/PA27).
BW16 exposes 13 GPIO on a 16-pad, 2 mm pitch module; no KiCad library symbol/footprint. No public chip exposed-pad dimension found.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather RP2040
boards.description: Feather-format RP2040 with 8 MB flash, USB-C, LiPo charger and STEMMA QT: the easiest way to get a Pico-class chip into the huge FeatherWing ecosystem.
notes: A0-A3 are all ADC inputs (a Pico exposes only three).
STEMMA QT connector shares the SDA/SCL header pins (I2C1, GPIO2/3).
Double-tap RESET or hold BOOT for the UF2 bootloader; the BOOT button is readable as a user button in CircuitPython.
16-pin header position 3 is a second 3V3 pin (no AREF).
USB-C connector overhangs the 50.8 mm Feather PCB by about 1.4 mm.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather RP2350 with HSTX Port
boards.description: Feather-format RP2350 with 8 MB flash, a 22-pin HSTX port for DVI video out, USB-C, LiPo charger and STEMMA QT; an 8 MB PSRAM version is sold separately.
notes: 29 GPIO = 21 on the Feather headers + 8 on the HSTX FPC connector (4 differential lanes, e.g. DVI via adapter).
Header pin 16 (GPIO8) is the PSRAM chip-select on the 8 MB PSRAM variant (product 6130, $15.50).
RP2350A (QFN-60); 8 MB QSPI flash.
16-pin header position 3 is a second 3V3 pin (no AREF).

boards.name: Adafruit Feather RP2040 CAN Bus
boards.description: RP2040 Feather with an MCP25625 (MCP2515 + transceiver) CAN 2.0B controller on SPI, 3.5 mm terminal block, switchable 120 ohm termination, 8 MB flash and LiPo charger.
notes: CAN is classic CAN 2.0B (no CAN-FD) up to 1 Mbit/s via an external SPI controller; chip-select GPIO19, interrupt GPIO22.
A 5 V charge pump (enabled by GPIO) powers the transceiver; CAN H/L/GND on a 3-pin 3.5 mm terminal block; 120 ohm termination jumper.
The terminal block makes the board about 12 mm tall.
The CAN control GPIOs (16-19, 22, 23) are used on-board and are not broken out to the Feather headers.

boards.name: Adafruit ESP32-S3 Feather (4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM)
boards.description: Dual-core ESP32-S3 Feather with native USB, Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5, 4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM, LiPo charger with fuel gauge and STEMMA QT with switchable power.
notes: MAX17048 battery fuel gauge on I2C; STEMMA QT power is switched by GPIO7 (I2C_POWER) for low-power sleep.
Native USB: hold BOOT while pressing RESET for the ROM/UF2 bootloader.
A cheaper 8 MB flash / no-PSRAM variant (product 5323) uses the same headers.
Header pin 'DB' is the debug UART TX (GPIO43). Frequently out of stock at Adafruit.

boards.name: Adafruit ESP32-S2 Feather (4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM)
boards.description: Single-core ESP32-S2 Feather (Wi-Fi 4, no BLE) with native USB, 4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM, LiPo charger with fuel gauge and STEMMA QT; solid for CircuitPython Wi-Fi projects.
notes: No Bluetooth (ESP32-S2 is Wi-Fi only).
STEMMA QT power and I2C pull-ups are gated by GPIO7: rev B board enables with LOW, rev C with HIGH.
Hold BOOT (DFU) while pressing RESET for the ROM bootloader.
Header pin 'DB' is the debug UART TX.

boards.name: Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2 (8 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM)
boards.description: Classic dual-core ESP32 (PICO-MINI-02 module) Feather with Wi-Fi 4 + Bluetooth Classic/LE, 8 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM, USB-C, LiPo charger and STEMMA QT.
notes: USB-UART bridge (CP2102N), not native USB; the original ESP32 has no USB OTG/UF2.
A2, A3, A4 and D37 (GPIO34/39/36/37) are input-only; ADC2 pins cannot be used while Wi-Fi is active.
Sold in PCB-antenna, w.FL-antenna and assembled-header versions.
User button on GPIO38; NeoPixel and STEMMA QT power switchable via GPIO2.

boards.name: Adafruit ESP32-C6 Feather (4 MB flash)
boards.description: Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5 and 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee/Matter) ESP32-C6 Feather with 4 MB flash, USB-C, LiPo charger with fuel gauge, STEMMA QT and a low-quiescent LDO for deep sleep.
notes: USB Serial/JTAG only (no USB OTG): CircuitPython cannot present a USB drive, use Wi-Fi/BLE/web workflow.
IO6 and IO5 are wired to both A2/A3 and the D6/D5 header positions, so 19 unique GPIO sit on 21 header pins.
Secondary low-quiescent LDO gives about 17 uA deep-sleep from LiPo.
Frequently out of stock at Adafruit.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather nRF52840 Express
boards.description: Bluetooth LE Feather with the nRF52840: native USB with UF2 bootloader, 2 MB QSPI flash for CircuitPython, LiPo charger, NeoPixel and SWD pads.
notes: Micro-USB (not USB-C) and no STEMMA QT/Qwiic connector.
1 MB internal flash plus 2 MB QSPI flash chip (CircuitPython filesystem).
Adafruit pin classes: 'LS' pins can interfere with the radio when toggled faster than ~10 kHz.
10-pin SWD connector footprint for a debugger. Frequently out of stock.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather M4 Express
boards.description: Fast, simple Feather with the ATSAMD51 (120 MHz Cortex-M4F), 2 MB QSPI flash for CircuitPython, 2 DACs, I2S and a LiPo charger.
notes: Micro-USB; no STEMMA QT connector. ATSAMD51J19 has 512 KB flash / 192 KB RAM; the 2 MB QSPI chip holds the CircuitPython filesystem.
DAC outputs on A0 and A1; 6 SERCOMs, I2S, parallel capture controller and hardware crypto.
Charger is 100 mA (slow); no fuel gauge.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather M4 CAN Express
boards.description: ATSAME51 (120 MHz Cortex-M4F) Feather using the chip's built-in CAN-FD controller with an on-board transceiver, 5 V booster and terminal block; 2 MB QSPI flash and USB-C.
notes: The transceiver is wired to CAN1 (PB14/PB15) with standby PB12 and booster enable PB13; CAN-FD works because it is the MCU's own controller.
3-pin 3.5 mm terminal block (CAN H/L/GND) with a 120 ohm termination jumper.
No STEMMA QT connector; charger is 100 mA.

boards.name: Adafruit Feather M0 Basic Proto
boards.description: Original Feather: ATSAMD21G18 (48 MHz Cortex-M0+) with USB, LiPo charger and a prototyping area; the cheapest classic Arduino-compatible Feather.
notes: 256 KB flash / 32 KB RAM and no external flash chip, so little room for CircuitPython scripts (the Express variants add 2 MB).
Micro-USB; last position of the 16-pin header is GND, not a GPIO.
DAC output on A0; 100 mA charger; no STEMMA QT connector.

boards.name: Adafruit QT Py RP2040
boards.description: XIAO-sized RP2040 with 8 MB flash, USB-C, NeoPixel and STEMMA QT port: a tiny Pico-class board with castellated pads.
notes: 13 GPIO = 11 on the pads + 2 on the STEMMA QT connector (separate I2C1 bus on GPIO22/23).
XIAO-compatible footprint and pad order; 5V pad is VBUS. 3.3 V regulator gives 600 mA peak.
Reset and BOOT buttons; A0-A3 are ADC inputs.
Listed length 21.8 mm includes the USB-C overhang; PCB outline used for the header coordinates is 20.7 mm.

boards.name: Adafruit QT Py ESP32-S3 (8 MB flash, no PSRAM)
boards.description: Tiny ESP32-S3 in the XIAO footprint with native USB-C, Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5, 8 MB flash, NeoPixel and STEMMA QT, castellated for direct PCB mounting.
notes: A 4 MB flash + 2 MB PSRAM version is sold as a separate product.
Native USB (UF2 / CircuitPython drive); BOOT button on GPIO0 plus RESET.
13 GPIO = 11 on pads + 2 on the STEMMA QT connector. Battery pads accept up to 6 V.
XIAO-compatible footprint and pad order; 5V pad is VBUS.
Frequently out of stock at Adafruit.

boards.name: Adafruit QT Py ESP32-C3
boards.description: RISC-V ESP32-C3 with Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5 in the XIAO footprint: 4 MB flash, USB-C, NeoPixel, STEMMA QT and castellated pads for under $10.
notes: USB Serial/JTAG only (no USB OTG): CircuitPython cannot present a USB drive, use Wi-Fi/BLE/web workflow.
Boot button on GPIO9 plus RESET.
13 GPIO listed by Adafruit = 11 pads + 2 extra; battery pads accept up to 6 V.
XIAO-compatible footprint and pad order; 5V pad is VBUS.
Frequently out of stock at Adafruit.

boards.name: Adafruit QT Py SAMD21
boards.description: Cheapest QT Py: ATSAMD21E18 (48 MHz Cortex-M0+) with USB-C, NeoPixel and STEMMA QT; unpopulated SOIC-8 pads on the back take an optional SPI flash.
notes: 256 KB flash / 32 KB RAM; only reset button (double-tap for the UF2 bootloader).
DAC on A0; I2S supported; 9 ADC pads.
XIAO-compatible footprint and pad order; 5V pad is VBUS.

boards.name: Adafruit ItsyBitsy M4 Express
boards.description: ATSAMD51 Cortex-M4F in a 35.6 x 17.8 mm breadboard-friendly board with 2 MB flash, 23 GPIO, 2 DACs, DotStar LED and a 5 V level-shifted D5 for NeoPixels.
notes: Header coordinates cover the two 14-pin rows only; D3, D4, EN and the SWD pads sit on an extra 5-pad edge at the far end.
D5 has a 3.3 V to 5 V level shifter (powered from the VHI pin) intended for NeoPixels.
Micro-USB; no LiPo charger (BAT is a power input only). 512 KB internal flash plus 2 MB QSPI flash.

boards.name: Adafruit Metro RP2350
boards.description: UNO-format RP2350B board with 16 MB flash, microSD, HSTX port for DVI video, STEMMA QT, USB-C and DC jack: shield-compatible and CircuitPython-friendly.
notes: Uses the 80-pin RP2350B (48 GPIO); A0-A5 are GPIO41-46.
37 GPIO per Adafruit = headers + 12 on the HSTX port + 2 for the USB host pads.
DC jack accepts 6-17 V; 3.3 V logic only (UNO shields must be 3.3 V compatible).
Ships with an RP2350 A2 stepping, which has documented GPIO/PIO errata. A PSRAM variant exists as a separate product.
UNO-style pin positions: digital headers along one long edge, power/analog on the other.

boards.name: Arduino Uno Rev3
boards.description: The reference Arduino: socketed ATmega328P, 5 V logic and the shield standard that thousands of tutorials and add-on boards assume.
notes: ATmega328P (DIP-28) is socketed and replaceable; USB goes through an ATmega16U2 so there is no native USB HID.
5 V logic, 20 mA per pin; only A0-A5 exist as analog inputs (A6/A7 are not on the DIP-28).
Barrel jack: 7-12 V recommended.
Only 32 KB flash and 2 KB RAM - Uno R4 Minima is a drop-in upgrade for a few dollars less.

boards.name: Arduino Uno R4 Minima
boards.description: Uno-shaped 5 V board with a 48 MHz Renesas RA4M1 Cortex-M4F, 256 KB flash, 12-bit DAC, CAN and native USB-C HID at a lower price than the Uno R3.
notes: 5 V logic but only 8 mA per I/O pin (not the 20 mA of the AVR Uno); VIN accepts 6-24 V.
12-bit DAC on A0, op-amp on A1-A3, CAN on D4 (TX)/D5 (RX) needs an external transceiver; RTC and SWD header on board.
Same shield footprint as the R3, but AVR-specific libraries/registers need porting.

boards.name: Arduino Uno R4 WiFi
boards.description: Uno R4 with an ESP32-S3 co-processor for WiFi and Bluetooth LE, a 12x8 LED matrix and a Qwiic connector on the same 5 V Uno shield footprint.
notes: The ESP32-S3 (3.3 V, level-shifted) is a separate chip that provides WiFi/BLE and USB-serial bridging; user code runs on the RA4M1.
12x8 red LED matrix is driven by dedicated RA4M1 pins, not the headers; Qwiic I2C connector is 3.3 V (Wire1).
VRTC pin backs up the RA4M1 RTC (no battery holder) and the OFF pin cuts board power; CAN on D10 (TX)/D13 (RX) needs an external transceiver.
5 V logic with 8 mA per pin max; VIN 6-24 V.

boards.name: Arduino Nano (ATmega328)
boards.description: The classic 45x18 mm breadboard-friendly Arduino: ATmega328, 5 V logic and 8 analog inputs on Mini-USB.
notes: Mini-USB; the official board uses an FTDI FT232 USB-serial chip (most clones use CH340/CP2102, which need drivers on some OSes).
A6/A7 are analog-only inputs; 5 V logic, VIN 6-20 V.
32 KB flash / 2 KB RAM - Nano Every and Nano R4 are cheaper and far more capable.

boards.name: Arduino Nano Every
boards.description: Cheap 5 V Nano with a 20 MHz ATmega4809 (48 KB flash, 6 KB RAM, UPDI) for about half the price of the classic Nano.
notes: A SAMD11 provides USB-serial and the UPDI programming path; the ATmega4809 itself has no USB.
Uses the megaAVR core, so libraries that poke ATmega328 registers directly may not work; 5 V logic, VIN 7-21 V.
Only one UART (Serial1) plus USB serial, one I2C and one SPI are broken out.

boards.name: Arduino Nano ESP32
boards.description: Nano-format ESP32-S3 (u-blox NORA-W106) with 16 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM, WiFi, BLE and USB-C, programmable with Arduino or MicroPython.
notes: 3.3 V logic only; VIN 6-21 V. Header pins use Arduino D#/A# names by default, not ESP32 GPIO numbers.
Native USB: double-tap reset for the DFU bootloader; also flashable with esptool-style tools and MicroPython.
ESP32-S3 sits in a u-blox NORA-W106 module with an on-board antenna; no external antenna connector.

boards.name: Arduino Nano 33 BLE Rev2
boards.description: Nano-format nRF52840 (u-blox NINA-B306) with BLE 5, 1 MB flash, 256 KB RAM and a 9-axis IMU (BMI270 + BMM150) at 3.3 V.
notes: 3.3 V logic only (not 5 V tolerant); VIN 5-18 V; Micro-USB.
IMU only (BMI270 + BMM150); the environmental sensors are on the separate Nano 33 BLE Sense Rev2.
nRF52840 sits in a u-blox NINA-B306 module with built-in antenna; frequently sold out at Arduino.

boards.name: Arduino Nano RP2040 Connect
boards.description: Nano-format RP2040 with 16 MB flash, u-blox NINA-W102 WiFi/Bluetooth, a 6-axis IMU and a microphone for around $21.
notes: A0-A3 use the RP2040 ADC; A4-A7 are read through the NINA-W102 ADC, and A4/A5 are shared with the I2C bus (4.7 kOhm pull-ups).
IMU is the LSM6DSOX; mic is the MP34DT06JTR; RGB LED is driven by the NINA module. 3.3 V logic, Micro-USB, VIN 4-20 V.
Short the REC pin to GND while resetting to enter the RP2040 ROM bootloader.

boards.name: Arduino Nano Matter
boards.description: Nano-format Silicon Labs MGM240S (EFR32MG24) with Thread, BLE 5.3 and Matter support, 1.5 MB flash and USB-C for $20.
notes: 3.3 V logic only; VIN up to 21 V; the 5V pin outputs 5 V only when USB powered.
Uses Silicon Labs MGM240SD22VNA (module with on-board antenna); Matter runs over Thread or BLE commissioning via the Arduino Matter library.
Note the UART is on D0 (TX) / D1 (RX), the reverse of classic Nano naming; Secure Vault High security.

boards.name: Arduino Nano R4
boards.description: Nano-format Renesas RA4M1 (48 MHz Cortex-M4F) at 5 V with USB-C, a Qwiic connector, DAC, CAN and RGB LED for about $12.
notes: 5 V I/O with a max of 8 mA per pin; VIN 6-21 V. The Qwiic port is a separate 3.3 V I2C bus (Wire1); header I2C (A4/A5) is 5 V.
Sold without headers ($12.10) or with headers ($13.30); castellated edge allows flat SMD mounting.
12-bit DAC on A0, op-amp on A1-A3, CAN on D4/D5 needs an external transceiver.

boards.name: Arduino Leonardo
boards.description: Uno-shaped 5 V board whose ATmega32U4 has native USB, so it can act as a keyboard, mouse or MIDI device without extra chips.
notes: Native USB HID/CDC on the ATmega32U4; no ATmega16U2, so the serial port disappears while the sketch resets USB.
12 analog inputs: A0-A5 plus A6-A11 shared with D4, D6, D8, D9, D10, D12; SDA/SCL also have dedicated header pins.
Only 32 KB flash (4 KB bootloader) and 2.5 KB RAM; Micro-USB.

boards.name: Arduino Micro
boards.description: Breadboard-sized 48x18 mm ATmega32U4 board with native USB HID, 20 I/O and 12 analog inputs at 5 V.
notes: Native USB (HID keyboard/mouse/MIDI); A6-A11 share digital pins; 5 V logic; Micro-USB.
Not pin-compatible with 'Pro Micro' clones despite the same chip - the header layout differs.

boards.name: Arduino Mega 2560 Rev3
boards.description: The big classic AVR board: ATmega2560 with 54 digital I/O, 16 analog inputs, 4 UARTs and 256 KB flash for printers, CNC and I/O-heavy projects.
notes: 54 digital I/O (15 PWM), 16 analog inputs, 4 hardware UARTs; USB via ATmega16U2; 5 V logic, 7-12 V recommended on the barrel jack.
Compatible with Uno shields plus the extra 36-pin double header; 8 KB SRAM is the practical limit.
Genuine boards are pricey - clones and Mega Pro boards cost far less.

boards.name: Arduino GIGA R1 WiFi
boards.description: Mega-sized 3.3 V board with dual-core STM32H747 (M7 480 MHz + M4 240 MHz), 16 MB QSPI flash, 8 MB SDRAM, WiFi/BLE, USB host and 76 I/O.
notes: 3.3 V logic only despite the Mega/Due shield layout. The M7 and M4 cores are programmed through Arduino's Mbed OS / Zephyr cores.
USB-A host + USB-C device, 3.5 mm audio jack on DAC0/DAC1/A7, 20-pin Arducam camera connector and MIPI-DSI display pins, ATECC608A secure element.
Wireless is a Murata 1DX (CYW4343W) with a u.FL antenna connector (antenna included); no Ethernet; CAN needs an external transceiver.
Big Arduino ecosystem but the Mbed-based core is heavier than bare-metal STM32 toolchains.

boards.name: Arduino UNO Q (2 GB)
boards.description: Dual-brain Uno-format board: Qualcomm QRB2210 running Debian plus an STM32U585 real-time MCU on 3.3 V Uno headers, with WiFi 5, BLE and an LED matrix.
notes: The MCU side (STM32U585, Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz, 2 MB flash, 786 KB RAM) runs Arduino Core on Zephyr; Linux, WiFi 5/BT 5.1, MIPI-CSI/DSI and the 2 GB LPDDR4 + 16 GB eMMC belong to the QRB2210 MPU.
Price rose from $44 to $59 in July 2026 (2 GB); the 4 GB / 32 GB variant is $79.
UNO headers are 3.3 V logic (A0, A1 and D3 are not 5 V tolerant); VIN 7-24 V; USB-C with PD and DisplayPort Alt-Mode. 8x13 blue LED matrix and Qwiic connector.
GPIO count covers D0-D13, D20/D21 (I2C), A0-A5 and the 3 dedicated JSPI pins; JMISC/JMEDIA expose more MCU and MPU signals.

boards.name: ESP32-DevKitC V4 (ESP32-DevKitC-32E)
boards.description: The reference classic-ESP32 board: WROOM-32E module (4 MB flash), USB-UART bridge, EN/BOOT buttons and 2x19 breadboard pins for about $10; pick it for Bluetooth Classic, DAC or the Ethernet MAC.
notes: Only a power LED (no user LED); the BOOT button (GPIO0) is the only user button.
D0-D3, CMD and CLK (GPIO6-11) are wired to the module flash and are not usable as GPIO, so 26 pins are really usable.
GPIO34-39 are input-only; ADC2 channels cannot be used while Wi-Fi is on; strapping pins are GPIO0, 2, 5, 12 (flash voltage) and 15.
Size includes the ~6 mm antenna overhang (PCB is 48.26 mm). Rows are 25.4 mm apart (1.0 in), wider than most breadboards leave room for.
Variants: -32E (4 MB), -VE (WROVER-E, 8 MB flash + 8 MB PSRAM, GPIO16/17 used by PSRAM), -32UE/-VIE (external antenna connector).

boards.name: ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 (N8R8)
boards.description: Official ESP32-S3 board with WROOM-1 N8R8 (8 MB flash, 8 MB octal PSRAM), native USB plus a UART bridge, addressable RGB LED and 2x22 breadboard pins; the default for S3/AI/camera/display work.
notes: Two Micro-USB ports: one through a CP2102N UART bridge, one wired to the S3 native USB (CDC/JTAG, GPIO19/20).
36 header GPIOs, but the N8R8 octal PSRAM/flash reserves GPIO35, 36 and 37, leaving 33 usable (N8/N8R2 modules keep them free).
Addressable RGB LED on GPIO38 (v1.1; v1.0 used GPIO48). Strapping pins: GPIO0, 3, 45, 46.
Size includes ~6 mm antenna overhang (PCB 62.74 mm). Many $7-12 AliExpress clones exist, often with USB-C and N16R8 modules; header order is the same.
Variants: -1U has an external antenna connector; N32R16V uses a WROOM-2 module.

boards.name: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 (N4X)
boards.description: Official $8 ESP32-C3 board: C3-MINI-1 module (4 MB flash), RGB LED, BOOT/RST buttons and 2x15 breadboard pins; the cheap RISC-V Wi-Fi + BLE 5 starting point with a KiCad footprint.
notes: Addressable RGB LED on GPIO8. GPIO8 and GPIO9 (the BOOT button) are strapping pins; GPIO2 is also a strapping pin.
USB goes through a CP2102N bridge; the native USB Serial/JTAG pins (GPIO18/19) are on the headers but not on the connector.
The original 4 MB ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 is obsolete; the N4X (in-package-flash MINI-1) is the current part. -1U has an external antenna connector.
Length includes ~5.5 mm antenna overhang (PCB 38.91 mm, estimated from the drawing).

boards.name: ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 (N8)
boards.description: Official ESP32-C6 board for about $9: Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5 and 802.15.4 (Thread/Zigbee/Matter) on a WROOM-1 module with 8 MB flash, two USB-C ports and 2x16 breadboard pins.
notes: Two USB-C ports: one via a CP2102N UART bridge, one native USB Serial/JTAG (GPIO12/13).
Addressable RGB LED on GPIO8. Strapping pins: GPIO4 (MTMS), 5 (MTDI), 8, 9 (BOOT button), 15.
J5 jumper allows current measurement of the module supply. -1U variant has an external antenna connector.
Length includes 6.35 mm antenna overhang (PCB 51.8 mm).

boards.name: ESP32-H2-DevKitM-1 (N4S)
boards.description: Official ESP32-H2 board (about $10): BLE 5 + 802.15.4 for Thread, Zigbee and Matter-over-Thread on an H2-MINI-1 module, two USB-C ports and 2x15 breadboard pins. No Wi-Fi.
notes: No Wi-Fi at all: use a C6 board if you need Wi-Fi plus Thread/Zigbee; the H2 is meant for Thread/Zigbee end devices and BLE.
Two USB-C ports: CP2102N UART bridge and native USB Serial/JTAG. Addressable RGB LED on GPIO8; GPIO8, 9 (BOOT) and 25 are strapping pins.
GPIO13/14 double as the optional 32.768 kHz crystal pins; the VBAT pin feeds the module RTC domain.
Length includes 5.4 mm antenna overhang (PCB 48.26 mm).

boards.name: ESP32-C5-DevKitC-1 (N8R8)
boards.description: Official $15 board for the ESP32-C5, the first Espressif chip with dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 6 plus BLE 5 and 802.15.4; 8 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM, two USB-C ports.
notes: Two USB-C ports: UART bridge and native USB Serial/JTAG. Addressable RGB LED on GPIO27.
Strapping pins: MTMS, MTDI, GPIO7, 25, 26, 27 and 28. The pin marked NC/15 is NC on PSRAM modules (N8R8), so 21 GPIOs are broken out.
Software support (ESP-IDF 5.5+, Arduino, esphome) is still maturing compared with C3/C6/S3.
Length includes 6.5 mm antenna overhang (PCB 53.6 mm). The older N8R4 variant is obsolete.

boards.name: ESP32-P4-Function-EV-Board (P4X)
boards.description: Multimedia board for the ESP32-P4: 16 MB flash, 32 MB PSRAM, MIPI-DSI 7-inch touch LCD, MIPI-CSI camera, 10/100 Ethernet, USB 2.0 HS host and Wi-Fi 6/BLE through a C6 co-processor.
notes: The ESP32-P4 has no radio: Wi-Fi 6 and BLE come from an on-board ESP32-C6-MINI-1 module connected over SDIO (ESP-Hosted), flashed separately.
The original board (P4 chip rev < 3) is obsolete; current stock is the ESP32-P4X-Function-EV-Board (chip rev 3.x). Match ESP-IDF/doc version to your chip revision.
Reference price is for the kit with the 7-inch 1024x600 touch LCD and 2 MP camera; the bare mainboard is not sold separately in most shops.
Ethernet is 10/100 (RMII, IP101 PHY). Three USB-C ports (UART/JTAG, full-speed, HS OTG) plus a USB 2.0 Type-A host port (shares the HS controller with the Type-C OTG port).
Size is the PCB outline taken from the Espressif DXF (approx.); 23 GPIOs on the 2x20 J1 header, many others used by on-board peripherals.

boards.name: ESP32-C3 SuperMini
boards.description: The default $2-3 ESP32-C3 board: 22.5 x 18 mm, USB-C, 4 MB flash, 13 GPIOs, BLE 5 and Wi-Fi; unbeatable on price, but with a weak ceramic antenna.
notes: Pin order with USB-C at the top: left column GPIO5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 20 (RX), 21 (TX); right column 5V, GND, 3V3, GPIO4, 3, 2, 1, 0. Row spacing is not published, so no carrier-board header data is provided.
ESP32-C3FH4 with 4 MB in-package flash. No UART bridge: native USB CDC/JTAG, so enable 'USB CDC On Boot' in Arduino; hold BOOT while plugging in if it is not detected.
Blue user LED on GPIO8 (shared with I2C SDA), red power LED. GPIO2, 8 and 9 are strapping pins (GPIO9 is the BOOT button).
The tiny ceramic antenna is the most common complaint (poor range, some batches badly tuned); a quarter-wave wire mod helps a lot.
Multiple look-alike clone batches exist with identical pinout; no official vendor page.

boards.name: ESP32-S3 SuperMini
boards.description: Thumb-sized ESP32-S3 board (S3FH4R2: 4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM) with USB-C and an RGB LED for about $5; dual-core S3 power in the SuperMini form factor.
notes: The 35 GPIOs counted by espboards.dev include pads on the underside; the two side headers alone carry fewer. Several different 'S3 SuperMini' layouts exist: check the pinout of your exact listing.
Embedded 2 MB quad PSRAM is disabled by default: enable 'QSPI PSRAM' in the Arduino tools menu or in ESPHome.
No UART bridge: enable 'USB CDC On Boot' for Serial output over the native USB port.
The red LED and the RGB LED share GPIO48. Some units ship with the ceramic antenna mounted wrongly (weak Wi-Fi); a ~31 mm wire antenna fixes it.
No official vendor page; data from espboards.dev.

boards.name: ESP32 DevKit V1 (DOIT, 30-pin)
boards.description: The ubiquitous $4-5 30-pin ESP32 devkit: WROOM-32 module, USB-UART bridge, EN/BOOT buttons and a blue LED; the cheapest classic ESP32 with Bluetooth Classic and DACs.
notes: 30-pin (2x15) version of the DOIT design: GPIO0 is not broken out and GPIO6-11 (flash) are absent, leaving 25 GPIOs. Many clones have 38 pins (DevKitC-like): count pins before buying.
USB-UART is CP2102 or CH340 depending on the batch (CH340 needs a driver on some OSes). Blue LED on GPIO2.
Some clones lack auto-reset and need BOOT held (or a ~10 uF cap EN-GND) during upload. GPIO34-39 are input-only; ADC2 is unusable while Wi-Fi is active.
Dimensions vary slightly between clone batches (about 51-55 mm long).

boards.name: Waveshare ESP32-S3-Zero
boards.description: Castellated 23.5 x 18 mm ESP32-S3FH4R2 board (4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM) with USB-C, WS2812 RGB LED and 24 GPIOs; the compact S3 for soldering straight onto a PCB.
notes: Pin order with USB-C at the top: left 5V, GND, 3V3(out), GP1-GP6; right TX, RX, GP13-GP7; GP14, 15, 16 on the bottom edge and GP17, 18, 38-42, 45 on underside pads. Rows are 15.24 mm apart (no mechanical drawing, so no header data).
WS2812 RGB LED data on GPIO21; BOOT and RESET buttons. Native USB only (no UART bridge): hold BOOT while plugging in to flash.
Sold without headers; the '-M' variant ships with headers soldered. Input 3.7-6 V on the 5V pad.

boards.name: Waveshare ESP32-C6-Zero
boards.description: Castellated 23.5 x 18 mm ESP32-C6FH8 board (8 MB in-package flash) with USB-C and WS2812 LED for about $5: Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5 and Thread/Zigbee in the smallest package.
notes: Pin order with USB-C at the top: left 5V, GND, 3V3(out), GP0-GP5; right TX, RX, GP14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22; GP6-9, 12, 13, 23 on underside pads. No mechanical drawing, so no header data.
WS2812 on GPIO8 and BOOT button on GPIO9 (strapping pins). Native USB Serial/JTAG on GPIO12/13 only, no UART bridge.
Sold without headers; a version with headers soldered costs about $1 more.

boards.name: Waveshare RP2040-Zero
boards.description: Postage-stamp RP2040 board (23.5 x 18 mm) with USB-C, 2 MB flash, WS2812 LED and castellated edges for under $4; 20 edge GPIOs plus 9 more on pads.
notes: Only 20 GPIOs (GP0-15, GP26-29) are on the castellated edge; GP17-GP25 are underside solder pads. GP16 drives the WS2812 RGB LED.
BOOT and RESET buttons give UF2 drag-and-drop programming. No SWD header.
Sold without headers ($3.99); a pre-soldered version is about $1 more. Header geometry taken from the Waveshare size drawing (2.54 mm castellated U-shape, rows 15.24 mm apart).

boards.name: Waveshare RP2350-Zero
boards.description: The RP2350 version of the Zero: 23.5 x 18 mm, USB-C, 2 MB flash, WS2812 LED and 20 castellated GPIOs (29 with pads) for under $5; dual Cortex-M33 / Hazard3 in a tiny board.
notes: RP2350A (30 GPIOs): GP0-15 and GP26-29 on the castellated edge, GP17-GP25 on underside pads, GP16 drives the WS2812 LED.
BOOT and RUN buttons give UF2 programming. No SWD header.
Sold without headers ($4.79); pre-soldered version about $1 more. Same footprint and pin order as the RP2040-Zero.

boards.name: LOLIN S2 Mini
boards.description: D1-mini-sized ESP32-S2FN4R2 board (4 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM) with USB-C, native USB and 27 GPIOs for about $5; cheap CircuitPython/USB-HID board, no Bluetooth.
notes: ESP32-S2 is single-core Xtensa with Wi-Fi 4 only (no Bluetooth). Native USB-OTG only, no UART bridge: hold button 0 and tap RST for the bootloader.
Compatible with LOLIN D1 mini shields (2x8 outer headers) but has 32 pins in total; DAC on GPIO17/18; blue LED on GPIO15.
No mechanical drawing for the extra pins, so no header data.

boards.name: LOLIN C3 Mini
boards.description: D1-mini-format ESP32-C3FH4 board (4 MB flash) with USB-C and a WS2812 RGB LED, compatible with the whole D1 mini shield ecosystem; 12 GPIOs for about $4.
notes: D1 mini shield compatible: 2x8 pins, rows 22.86 mm apart. Pin names (D0-D8, D10) are the LOLIN labels, not GPIO numbers; header data is taken from the official KiCad footprint/symbol.
Native USB Serial/JTAG only (no UART bridge): hold BOOT while plugging in to flash.
Header start offset (7.75 mm from the antenna end) is read from the KiCad footprint outline.

boards.name: LOLIN (WEMOS) D1 mini
boards.description: The classic $2-4 ESP8266 board: 4 MB flash, CH340 USB, 11 GPIOs and the biggest shield ecosystem (OLED, relay, SD, battery); the cheapest Wi-Fi board that still has loads of tutorials.
notes: ESP8266EX, 3.3 V only. Single 10-bit ADC (A0, max 3.2 V via on-board divider). D0 (GPIO16) has no PWM/I2C/interrupt; D3, D4 (LED) and D8 are strapping pins.
The current official LOLIN V4 has USB-C; the common $2 clones are Micro-USB with CH340C or CP2104 (CH340 driver needed on some OSes).
2x8 header, rows 22.86 mm apart (header data from the official KiCad footprint: first pin 8.21 mm from the antenna end). ESP8266 is legacy; a C3 mini is a better buy for new designs.

boards.name: NodeMCU V3 (ESP-12E, CH340)
boards.description: Cheap ESP8266 devkit (ESP-12E, CH340G, micro-USB) with all pins broken out on 2x15 headers and FLASH/RST buttons; the long-time Lua/Arduino Wi-Fi beginner board at about $3.5.
notes: 11 usable GPIOs (D0-D8, RX, TX); two more (SD2/SD3 = GPIO9/10) are usable only in DIO flash mode. Single 10-bit ADC on A0 (0-1 V on the chip, 3.3 V via divider on most boards).
The 'V3' LoLin board is 31 mm wide and covers a whole breadboard; the V2 'Amica' board is 26 mm and breadboard-friendly.
CH340G driver needed on some OSes. Legacy chip: prefer ESP32-C3 boards for new projects.

boards.name: Blue Pill (STM32F103C8T6)
boards.description: The $2-3 STM32F103 Cortex-M3 board: 72 MHz, 64/128 KB flash, 2x20 breadboard pins, micro-USB; the cheapest ARM board, but older and full of clone-chip and USB-resistor gotchas.
notes: Genuine ST chips are rare: many boards carry CKS32F103, APM32F103 or GD32F103 clones (some with 128 KB flash enabled); behaviour and USB can differ.

The USB D+ pull-up resistor (R10) is often 10 k instead of 1.5 k, which breaks USB enumeration on some hosts; swap it. No ROM USB DFU on F103: flash with ST-Link (SWD header) or the UART bootloader (BOOT0 jumper).
5 V pins connect straight to USB VBUS with no protection. PC13 LED is active-low. No mechanical drawing verified, so no header data.
For a modern replacement use a WeAct Black Pill (F411/G431) at similar cost.

boards.name: WeAct Black Pill V3.1 (STM32F411CEU6)
boards.description: Best-value STM32 board: 100 MHz Cortex-M4F with FPU, 512 KB flash, USB-C and ROM DFU on a breadboard-friendly 2x20 board for about $6; the Blue Pill done right.
notes: F411 has a ROM USB DFU bootloader: hold BOOT0 and tap NRST. Blue LED on PC13 (active low), KEY button on PA0, 4-pin SWD header (3V3/SWDIO/SWCLK/GND) on the board.
V3.x uses a 25 MHz HSE crystal (set HSE_VALUE accordingly); the optional SPI flash footprint (U3) is unpopulated. The same board is also sold with STM32F401CC/CE.
Beware of counterfeit look-alikes without the 'WeAct Studio' logo and version silk. PA13/PA14 are on the SWD header only (not on the 2x20 headers).
Header positions come from the WeAct board-shape drawing (rows 15.2 mm apart, first pin 1.5 mm from the USB end).

boards.name: WeAct STM32G474 Core Board
boards.description: Compact STM32G474CEU6 board (170 MHz Cortex-M4F, 512 KB flash, 128 KB RAM) with USB-C and two 2x12 headers for about $6; analog/motor-control/HRTIM chip very cheaply.
notes: Two double-row (2x12) headers along the long sides plus a 4-pin SWD header; NRST, BOOT0 and a user button. No ST-LINK on board: use an external SWD probe or the ROM USB DFU (BOOT0).
USB, CAN-FD, 5 ADCs, 4 DACs, op-amps and the HRTIM are all available on the headers; there is no CAN transceiver. PA11/PA12 are shared between USB and CAN.
GPIO count is 37 broken-out GPIOs (UFQFPN48 has 38). Cheaper STM32G431CBU6 and a 'Long' G474CBT6 variant exist: check the exact listing.
No header data: double-row layout not verified.

boards.name: WeAct BluePill Plus CH32V203
boards.description: RISC-V Blue Pill replacement: CH32V203C8T6 (144 MHz QingKe V4B, 64 KB flash, 20 KB RAM, USB FS) on a USB-C 2x20 board for about $4; very cheap fast RISC-V with USB.
notes: Same 52.81 x 20.78 mm board as the Black Pill but with the classic Blue Pill pin order (NRST/PB11/PB10 near the 3V3 pin). Header positions assume the Black Pill geometry (rows 15.2 mm apart).
User KEY on PA0, blue LED on PB2 (active high); 4-pin SWD header. Program with a WCH-LinkE (SWD/SDI) or WCHISPTool; unpopulated SPI flash footprint (U3).
Also sold with CH32F103, CH32V103 and CH32V303 chips on the same PCB. Toolchain support: MounRiver Studio, Arduino core (ch32-community), PlatformIO.

boards.name: nanoCH32V003 (MuseLab)
boards.description: Tiny breadboard board for the 10-cent CH32V003F4U6 (48 MHz RISC-V, 16 KB flash) with USB-C power, 24 MHz crystal, reset button and LED; the cheapest way to try the CH32V003.
notes: The USB-C port is power only (CH32V003 has no USB): programming needs a WCH-LinkE (about $5) on the 3-pin SWIO header. Budget for that.

Two rows of 11 pins at 2.54 mm (top: G, C4-C0, D0, 3V3, A2, A1, D1; bottom: G, 5V, C5-C7, D2-D7) plus a 3-pin GND/SWIO/3V3 programming header; QFN-20 chip. The same PCB takes CH32V002F4U6 / CH32V004F6U1.
Size, price and I/O voltage are estimates from product photos; no official dimension drawing found.

boards.name: Digispark ATtiny85 USB
boards.description: The $1.50-2 USB-stick ATtiny85 board with the Micronucleus bootloader: plug into any USB-A port, no programmer needed; ideal for tiny USB gadgets, 5 usable I/O and about 6 KB of flash.
notes: Micronucleus USB bootloader (software USB, V-USB): uploads via micronucleus/Arduino with no programmer, ~6 KB usable flash, bootloader waits ~5 s after plug-in.
P0-P5 are GPIO but P3/P4 are the USB lines and P5 is RESET; using P5 as GPIO needs the RSTDISBL fuse (removes the ability to reflash). In practice 5 usable pins.
Many clones ship with weak USB regulators/zeners and need a short USB extension to enumerate reliably. Micro-USB versions exist. Dimensions approximate.
digistump.com was unreachable when this was checked; the Arduino core is on GitHub.

boards.name: Arduino Pro Mini clone (ATmega328P)
boards.description: Ultra-cheap $2-3 ATmega328P Uno-class board in a 33 x 18 mm package with 20 I/O and 8 ADC channels; no USB, so budget a $1-2 serial adapter, but ideal for permanent low-power projects.
notes: No USB: program through the 6-pin header with an FTDI/CH340/CP2102 adapter (DTR auto-reset). The adapter is not included.
Two versions: 5 V / 16 MHz and 3.3 V / 8 MHz; I/O voltage follows the version (table lists the 5 V one). Check the regulator/resonator markings.
14 digital pins and 6 analog pins (A0-A5) are usable as GPIO; A6/A7 are analog-input only (extra ADC channels). I2C is A4/A5 on inner pads.
Clone quality varies (ceramic resonator, counterfeit 328 chips); no header data due to the 4-group (sides, FTDI, inner pad) layout.

boards.name: nice!nano v2
boards.description: The wireless-keyboard standard: nRF52840 in a Pro Micro footprint with USB-C, LiPo charger, UF2 bootloader and very low idle current; drop-in for Pro Micro boards (ZMK/QMK).
notes: Pro Micro pin-compatible but 3.3 V logic (not 5 V tolerant). Adafruit UF2 bootloader: double-tap reset to mount as a drive.

P0.13 on the VCC pin switches the 3.3 V rail for external peripherals; P0.04 reads battery voltage and cannot be used otherwise. Charger supports 4.2 V LiPo via solder pads (100/500 mA); no connector.
About $25 at nicekeyboards.com (price not shown on the product page, verify). Many cheaper 'SuperMini nRF52840' clones exist.
No header data: pin order not verified from an official drawing.

boards.name: SuperMini nRF52840 (nice!nano clone)
boards.description: $5 clone of the nice!nano v2: nRF52840 with USB-C, LiPo charging on BAT pads and the Adafruit UF2 bootloader in a Pro Micro-compatible layout; cheapest BLE 5 board with 1 MB flash.
notes: Clone of the nice!nano v2 layout (Pro Micro-compatible pinout); no vendor page: the nice!nano page is the reference design. Dimensions, LED and charger details vary by seller, and some 'SuperMini nRF52840' listings are a smaller ~22 mm board: check the listing.
Adafruit nRF52 UF2 bootloader: double-tap reset to mount as a drive. Works with ZMK, Arduino (Adafruit nRF52 core) and Zephyr.
Battery pads (BAT+/BAT-) with an on-board charger; some clones omit the VCC switch (P0.13) or the battery-voltage divider (P0.04) that nice!nano has.
Size, GPIO count and price are estimates for the Pro Micro form factor.

boards.name: Sipeed Longan Nano (GD32VF103CBT6)
boards.description: Cheap RISC-V board with a 0.96-inch 160x80 IPS LCD, microSD slot, USB-C and GD32VF103CBT6 (108 MHz, 128 KB flash, 32 KB RAM, USB DFU) for about $5-6.
notes: Program over USB DFU (hold BOOT, tap reset, dfu-util) or the serial ISP; the 2x4 JTAG header needs a RISC-V debug probe. Supported by PlatformIO, Arduino-style cores and the GD32VF103 SDK.
Seeed's listing ($4.90) is marked discontinued; Sipeed's AliExpress store and other resellers still sell it. Some variants omit the LCD.
Board size is approximate (not stated on the Sipeed page); 28 GPIOs are led out to two pin headers.

boards.name: Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 (V3)
boards.description: ESP32-S3 + SX1262 LoRa board with 0.96-inch OLED, LiPo charger and USB-C for about $18; the go-to cheap Meshtastic/LoRaWAN node with Wi-Fi and BLE.
notes: ESP32-S3FN8 (8 MB in-package flash), SX1262 LoRa (buy the 433, 470-510, 863-870 or 902-928 MHz version for your region), 0.96-inch 128x64 OLED, CP2102 USB-UART plus native USB.
LoRa antenna goes on the U.FL/IPEX connector: always attach it before transmitting. SH1.25-2 LiPo connector with on-board charging; Vext pin switches a 3.3 V rail for sensors.
28 GPIOs on the 2x18 headers, several of which drive on-board parts (OLED on 17/18/21, LED 35, Vext 36, USB 19/20, PRG button 0). V3.1/V3.2 revisions differ slightly (LoRa power, ADC control).
Price range $17.90-19.90 at Heltec depending on band and accessories.

boards.name: LILYGO T-Display S3
boards.description: ESP32-S3R8 board with a 1.9-inch 170x320 color LCD, 16 MB flash, 8 MB octal PSRAM, USB-C, LiPo connector and Qwiic port for about $9; best value S3 board with a built-in screen.
